articles.title: Controlling Unalienable Rights
articles.author: Chuck Yates
articles.content: The opinions expressed here are solely the author's and do not reflect the opinions or beliefs of the LA Progressive. Early voting opened here in Idaho on October 19, and we were among the first to go in and exercise our franchise. The ballot this time includes four measures for voters to consider. One is an invitation to designate the official state gun. Choices include one modern rifle, two World War II icons, and three Wild West classics. In a state where six of every ten people own guns, this measure is not surprising. The others are less frivolous. Two of them would amend the state constitution in consequential ways. House Joint Resolution 4 would grant the legislature sole authority to legalize marijuana and other psychoactive substances, depriving voters of any further say in the matter. House Joint Resolution 6 would make English the official language of the state, requiring all official and public business to be conducted in only in that language. The fourth measure, Proposition 1, “The Reproductive Freedom and Privacy Act,” would alleviate some of the state’s restrictions on abortion. As set forth in the current law, Title 18-622, “The Defense of Life Act,” abortion is legal in Idaho only in cases of medical emergency, rape, or incest. A physician may act to save the life of the mother, but survivors of rape or incest must report incidents and provide official documentation within the first thirteen weeks. Related: The National Anthem and America's Dangerous Brand of Patriotism Title 18-622 complicates the lives of those in need of an abortion, but it’s not aimed at them. It’s aimed at everyone involved in performing abortions. The law classifies abortion as a felony, and those convicted of performing it or assisting in its performance would spend two to five years in prison, and could lose their licenses to practice medicine in Idaho. Thus it’s no surprise that over a third of the state’s ob/gyn specialists have either left or stopped practicing. Ostensibly, the intent of 18-622 is to defend the life of the fetus in the womb. But it does not defend the life of a fetus in the womb of a woman whose own life is endangered, or in the womb of a survivor of rape or incest. Depending on circumstances, then, the lives of some fetuses are just not worthy of defense. In other words, the “defense of life” ordained by 18-622 is not “pro-life.” In some cases, as specified in the statute, it’s actually anti-life. Proposition 1 would create a new chapter in the Idaho statutes, not in Title 18, “Crimes and Punishments,” but in Title 39, “Health and Safety.” It would establish a right “to make private reproductive health care decisions, including abortion up to fetal viability and in medical emergencies....Notwithstanding any other provision of law to the contrary....”—that is, regardless of anything in 18-622. The new law, Title 39-8, would retain the restrictions imposed by 18-622, limiting abortion to the first trimester, with exceptions only to save the mother’s life or in cases of rape or incest. But it would decriminalize the performance of abortions, and it would remove the threat of imprisonment and loss of professional credentials for those performing them. And it would restore individual agency. Note well: the restrictions on abortion itself would not change, only the state-imposed social control. Related: Major Jason Watson, Trump, and the Military’s Duty to Defy Illegal Orders Specifically, Title 39-8 “recognizes that reproductive health care choices...are deeply private matters,” and it “upholds a person’s rights to make their own decisions based on their own values, health care needs, and circumstances—free from the fear of external pressures or punitive consequences....” The choice would be that of the pregnant woman and no one else. No parent, guardian, public official, or sexual partner would have any role in the matter, unless invited to participate. Opponents of Proposition 1 claim that it would establish “abortion on demand,” and turn abortion into an unregulated free for all. More likely, what they object to is the assumption behind its key terms, “personal” and “private.” It would eliminate the right of the state, and of individuals, to interfere in a process that properly involves only the person going through it and those assisting her. In other words, the controversy likely isn’t as much about abortion as it is about who gets to decide, and who doesn’t. Opponents of abortion have their reasons, and certainly no one actually approves of or desires abortion, except as a justified last resort. For some, abortion is an atrocity, not different from the Final Solution except in magnitude. For others, it’s more analogous to an amputation, deeply tragic but in some cases necessary. In the end, what it comes down to is that a patriarchal surveillance state cannot permit its subjects to enjoy liberties such as those specified in Proposition 1. The existing law effectively deprives everyone in Idaho of exactly those liberties defined elsewhere as “unalienable rights” to “life, liberty, and the pursuit of happiness.” The chief purpose of Proposition 1 is to restore those rights.

articles.title: Trump Is Helping Putin
articles.author: Mel Gurtov
articles.content: The opinions expressed here are solely the author's and do not reflect the opinions or beliefs of the LA Progressive. In the past week the President of the US has revealed his true colors on Russia’s war more clearly than ever. The rift between Trump and Ukraine’s President Volodymyr Zelensky has grown very wide—much wider than in February 2025 when Trump admonished Zelensky in the White House for being ungrateful about US aid–and might not be bridgeable. Ukraine: Now Putin’s and Trump’s Common Enemy The signs of the rift are clear enough: · Trump is putting money in Russia’s hands with a major oil deal that involves both family members (Jared Kushner), members of his inner circle (Steve Witkoff), and various Middle East sheikhs and investors. The deal is backed by the US International Finance Development Corporation, the same agency that manages the 2025 US-Ukraine minerals deal. The deal will involve a takeover of the Lukoil conglomerate’s refineries, distributors, and gas stations. · Trump’s plan to import Russian diesel oil will provide Russia with billions of dollars that can be used to support its war effort. It’s a major shot in the arm for Russia’s failing economy. The ink was barely dry on the recent bipartisan bill that is supposed to impose sanctions on Russia–named for Sen. Lindsey Graham—when Trump eviscerated it. By executive order, he waived sanctions on Russia. · Trump’s proposal for a Ukraine-Russia “energy cease-fire” was greeted with bewilderment by Zelensky, since Russia has never agreed to any kind of cease-fire and, to the contrary, has significantly expanded its missile and drone attacks on Ukraine’s cities. Vladimir Putin has not hidden his strategy of making the upcoming winter so miserable for Ukrainians, by attacking electricity and power stations, that they will force the government to sue for peace on Russia’s terms. Related: Trump and Xi Talk Stability as China’s Global Leverage Grows Trump has said Ukraine needs a new president—obviously, one more compliant than Zelensky. Trump has said it’s “a disgrace” that Ukraine is continuing to attack Russian fuel depots and thus creating US and global diesel shortages. Evidently, Russian attacks on Ukraine that have caused electrical outages affecting hundreds of thousands of households, not to mention lives, are not a disgrace. (Also disgraceful is that Trump has failed to acknowledge that it’s his war on Iran that is the primary reason for fuel shortages.) · The Pentagon, evidently at Trump’s order, has limited intelligence sharing with Ukraine on incoming Russian missiles (though it claims to have restored it), demanded that countries with Patriot air defense systems stop providing them to Ukraine, and, at Elon Musk’s urging, has limited Ukraine’s use of the Starlink system for military communications. It’s Up to Europe All these developments have made all-out European support of Ukraine absolutely essential. The Trump administration cannot be relied on even for those few things—such as sales of weapons to European countries for turnover to Ukraine—that are still supposedly part of US policy. NATO’s role in European security now has to mean Europe alone; Trump, a longtime critic of NATO (and all other security coalitions), is oblivious to Russia’s threat to Europe and cannot be counted on to help confront Russia’s intensifying hybrid warfare. Europe will have to do much more than it is now doing. Up to now, it has contributed about €228 billion since the start of the war in 2022, including nearly €100 billion in military aid. Assistance for humanitarian and economic reconstruction programs adds to these figures. Germany and the UK are among the top donors. If aid as a proportion of GDP is the standard, Denmark and Estonia are the most generous. In comments over the weekend, European leaders vowed to step up aid to Ukraine and maintain sanctions on Russia. But if right-wing political parties prevail in German, French, and other European elections, the European Union will have great difficulty mustering additional support for Ukraine. Related: Losing Hand in the Iran War With winter coming, life in Ukraine will be more difficult than ever. Russian attacks will create major power outages, blockages of truck traffic to deliver goods, and more obstacles to obtaining health care and education for children. And there will be many more casualties. On the battlefield, unless the Starlink system is fully restored, Ukraine’s military, which had kept Russian forces from advancing over the past year, may have to give up territory. Its one source of leverage will be the ability to attack Russian oil refineries, causing long lines at the pump for Russians and potentially anger at Putin for pursuing his aggressive war. In Putin’s Pocket A Washington Post report on October 21 said that at a meeting in Oslo with European representatives as well as Witkoff, a US official said: “Ukraine brought forward new ideas and proposals, which were discussed in detail. The parties made meaningful progress in aligning on a coordinated approach to engaging Russia and advancing the diplomatic process.” The official also said that there was “strong alignment” among the US, Ukraine, and Europe on the next steps, and that Witkoff and Kushner would push Putin to hold “direct trilateral” talks with Zelensky and Trump. I have serious doubts that “strong alignment” exists, that Putin is being pushed, or that Russia will be interested in direct talks so long as Trump keeps providing new incentives for it to win “peace” on Russian terms. Besides, Trump keeps singing a different tune, saying (like Moscow) that Ukraine is the main obstacle to a peace agreement and that Russia is winning the war on the ground: “What’s happening is that Russia would like to get it done,” Trump told reporters in the Oval Office on Tuesday after the meeting: “Russia is a big machine. They just keep grinding forward. … They’ve taken a very large piece of land, and you know, you can say that Ukraine is doing well or poorly, but the land gets bigger and bigger all the time, week by week.” Speaking outside a campaign rally, Trump also said: “Russia, frankly, has been fine on Ukraine. They haven’t been doing much.” On the other hand: “We’ve given a lot to Ukraine. They’ve given nothing to us. Remember that.” Can you imagine such callous indifference to reality? Related: Weapons, War and Profit: Inside the $2.9 Trillion Global Arms Race Make no mistake: the Trump administration has become partners with Putin in this aggression. To have Witkoff call Putin a “humanitarian” in the mold of Trump seals the deal. Trump will rant and rail at Zelensky for causing a diesel shortage and rejecting a cease-fire, but even many of Trump’s allies in Congress now see clearly that Trump is Putin’s key enabler—that Trump is not merely siding with Putin on diplomatic matters and ignoring the horrific damage Russian attacks have caused in Ukraine; his administration is directly funding Russia’s war. As Zelensky has said, “At this very moment, while we are talking about peace, America is allowing Russia to export diesel… all of that money goes toward the war against people, against Ukraine, against all of us.” That betrayal, to my mind, constitutes treachery and should be part of impeachment proceedings after the November elections. Peace Voice

articles.title: Hell Is Real
articles.author: Eva Amar
articles.content: The opinions expressed here are solely the author's and do not reflect the opinions or beliefs of the LA Progressive. In 2010, I was driving along Interstate 65 toward Bloomington, Indiana, when an enormous roadside billboard caught my attention. HELL IS REAL. I was returning to Indiana University, where my daughter had been raped four years earlier. Of all the messages I might have encountered along that highway, those three words seemed almost deliberately placed in my path. Back in the mid-1970s, when I worked as a systems support technician, my colleagues nicknamed me “Queen Irony.” If I said the sky was blue, it would almost immediately turn black and start pouring. The irony of that billboard was certainly not lost on me. I'd made that trip many times, returning for Take Back the Night rallies and other efforts to confront campus sexual violence. By then, I'd learned that my daughter's experience was hardly unique. In 2006, weeks before finishing her freshman year at Indiana University, my daughter called me, sobbing. She had been raped. Related: Charity Begins at Home What followed was an education I never wanted, membership in a club I never imagined joining, and a painful awakening to the failures of a system I had trusted to protect my daughter. I learned that the man she accused had a prior felony battery conviction and had been placed on a three-day psychiatric hold. There had been troubling incidents involving other young women. Yet he had been allowed to return to a coeducational residence hall. Evidence wasn't properly preserved. Prosecutors declined charges. The university carried on. My daughter survived. But what I learned about the institutions entrusted with protecting young women changed the direction of my life. A College Campus Is No Ivory Tower College is supposed to be a young woman's introduction to independence, not her introduction to sexual violence. Twenty-six years ago, the U.S. Department of Justice warned that between one-fifth and one-quarter of college women could be expected to experience completed or attempted rape during their college careers. Parents worry about tuition, roommates, grades, and whether their daughters are eating properly. Perhaps we should spend more time asking whether the universities collecting those tuition checks are doing their jobs. Indiana University wasn't unique. In 2000, student Jill Behrman disappeared while bicycling. Her remains were discovered years later. In 2011, Lauren Spierer disappeared after a night out in Bloomington. Her disappearance remains unsolved. Lauren's parents have spent fifteen years without an answer to the most basic question imaginable: Where is our daughter? At the University of North Carolina Wilmington, two young women were murdered just 30 days apart in 2004. Related: Don't Look Down: America's Democracy Is Under Strain—and the World Is Watching On May 5, Jessica Faulkner was raped and murdered in her dormitory by fellow student Curtis Dixon, who had a history of stalking and threatening women at other universities. That history had not been disclosed on his application to UNCW. I spoke with Jessica's father, John Faulkner. It was a painful conversation on many levels, one I have never forgotten. John subsequently advocated for stronger criminal-background screening at North Carolina universities, hoping to prevent another family from experiencing what his had endured. You might think Jessica's murder would have put an entire university on heightened alert. But just weeks later, Christen Naujoks and her mother sought help from campus police because Christen was being stalked and threatened by a former boyfriend. According to her mother's account, when they requested a different parking space for Christen's protection, they were reportedly told that changing hers would mean changing everyone's. This was the same university where a young woman had just been murdered. Christen obtained a protective order. It didn't save her. On June 4, 2004, she was shot to death outside her apartment. Two young women. One university. Thirty days. I haven't forgotten Jessica Faulkner or Christen Naujoks, and I never will. [PHOTOGRAPHS TO INSERT: Jessica Faulkner and Christen Naujoks, side by side] At Notre Dame, Lizzy Seeberg reported a sexual assault involving a football player in 2010. She faced intimidating messages afterward and died by suicide days later. At the University of Virginia, Yeardley Love was murdered by her former boyfriend in 2010. At the University of Utah, Lauren McCluskey was murdered in 2018 after repeatedly seeking help concerning threats from a former boyfriend. More than twenty years have passed since Jessica and Christen were murdered. Yet the systemic indifference their cases exposed remains disturbingly familiar in the handling of sexual violence allegations at Cornell University today. He Said. He Said. For years, police and prosecutors explained to me why sexual assault cases couldn't move forward. He said. She said. I eventually wrote an article called He Said. He Said. because that familiar expression doesn't accurately describe what happens. The accused says the encounter was consensual. And too often, that's where the investigation begins and ends. There is no meaningful she said. Whatever she says seems to carry little weight against his assertion of consent. At Cornell University, a young woman has alleged that she was gang raped by fraternity members who, according to her account, used social media to invite other men to join them while the assault was taking place. How morally depraved would you have to be to participate in something like that? According to reporting on the case, the prosecutor declined criminal charges without personally interviewing the complainant or reviewing her complete interview transcript. Apparently, hearing from the woman herself wasn't considered essential. And we're still calling this He Said. She Said. Related: He said. He said. End of Story. A New Generation, the Same Old Misogyny What troubles me about the Cornell allegations goes beyond the alleged assault itself. It's the suggestion that violence against a woman could become a spectacle, something to share, even an invitation for others to participate. What kind of culture produces that attitude toward women? Perhaps we shouldn't be surprised when men like Andrew and Tristan Tate cultivate enormous audiences while promoting deeply troubling attitudes toward women. Both face serious criminal charges in the United Kingdom involving alleged sexual violence and trafficking. They deny wrongdoing and are entitled to the presumption of innocence. But their criminal cases are only part of the story. What troubles me is the audience for a brand of masculinity that treats domination as strength and women as something to be controlled. We spent generations telling our daughters they deserved equality. Who is telling our sons that equality isn't an insult? Today we have domestic violence laws, sexual assault statutes, Title IX, the Clery Act, and enough university policies to wallpaper a football stadium. We've made progress in legislation. I'm considerably less impressed with our progress in accountability. Justice Delayed Is Justice Denied And what happens when women turn to the agencies charged with holding these institutions accountable? Apparently, they wait. And wait. At Lehigh University, where nineteen-year-old Jeanne Clery was raped and murdered in her residence hall in 1986, a federal complaint has reportedly remained unresolved for six years. It was Jeanne's murder that led her parents to fight for the federal campus crime reporting law that bears her name. Even at the university where that tragedy occurred, the system established in its aftermath appears unable to deliver timely accountability. At George Mason University, a woman who had survived sexual violence had neither the strength nor the emotional reserves to pursue a complaint against the man she accused. But when she learned that the man she identified as her assailant, who had a serious criminal history, had obtained a teaching position, she found the courage to come forward. Not for herself, but because she feared for the young women who might find themselves in his classroom. Nearly four years later, according to her account, her federal Clery Act complaint remains unresolved. She says she has received neither meaningful protection nor justice, while the man she accused has gone on to pursue a law degree. She came forward to protect others. Who has protected her? We created a system to police the institutions that failed to protect these women. But who is policing that system? Of All Places, Safety Harbor The failure to protect women isn't confined to university campuses. It follows them into their homes, their relationships, and sometimes to their graves. On October 13, 2026, in a Florida town called Safety Harbor, 30-year-old Jessica Antolini was shot in the face and then run over by a vehicle, allegedly driven by her assailant. Her boyfriend, Christopher “Dodge” Smith, has been charged with first-degree murder and child abuse. He is presumed innocent unless convicted. Jessica died two days later. Smith's five-year-old daughter and their dog were in the vehicle when police located it. I cannot stop thinking about that little girl and what she may have seen or heard that night. Five years old. What kind of memories will she carry into adulthood? And of all places, Safety Harbor. Women can report abuse, seek restraining orders, file complaints, and invoke federal protections. But those protections mean little when the people responsible for enforcing them fail to act. Jessica Antolini is dead. And countless women are still waiting for somebody to take their complaints seriously. I still remember that billboard on Interstate 65. HELL IS REAL. For the women who have endured violence, the families who have buried daughters, and the children left behind, it isn't a theological argument. It's something they've lived. October will end, as it always does. But we should remember what this month represents, not just during October, but during the other eleven months of the year. It's been twenty years since my daughter was raped. We've made progress, but nowhere near enough, and nowhere near fast enough. I can only hope that twenty years from now, no one will still have reason to write this same article.

articles.title: Generation Revolts Against Capitalism
articles.author: Henry A. Giroux
articles.content: The opinions expressed here are solely the author's and do not reflect the opinions or beliefs of the LA Progressive. Across France, Spain, India, Italy, Albania, and other parts of the world, young people are taking to the streets, giving voice to a growing international revolt against the collapse of social protections, the underfunding of education, the erosion of democratic rights, and the cruel politics of austerity. Despite their different national histories, these struggles share a growing anger at the savage machinery of neoliberal capitalism, its abandonment of the young, its concentration of wealth and power in the hands of ruling elites, its embrace of militarism, and its systematic destruction of the public institutions and social protections on which democratic life depends. Young people are rising against the colonial plunder, obscene inequalities, systemic corruption, ecological devastation, endless wars, and fascist culture and pedagogy that have robbed them of their dignity, stolen their hopes, and threatened to write them out of history. They are refusing to surrender their right to a future. In France, what began as protests against overcrowded classrooms, deteriorating schools, and teacher shortages has grown into a nationwide movement drawing support from parents, university students, workers, and trade unions. Barricades are now up in France The deeper significance of this revolt lies in its growing recognition that the crisis of education is inseparable from a global capitalist system that has turned the future itself into a site of dispossession, condemning young people to lives increasingly defined by insecurity, precarity, and the threat of social abandonment. Writing in The Nation, Harrison Stetler and June Loper place the French student revolt within a widening international struggle among young people confronting a capitalist system that has robbed them of economic security, political agency, and the promise of a livable future. They write: A segregated, underfunded education system is only one of the many grievances bringing French high school and university students out in force. From artificial intelligence and climate change to diminishing expectations over an uncertain future, they are calling attention to many of the demands heard in youth-led movements like Spain’s recent housing protests, anti-conscription demonstrations in Germany, and India’s so-called “cockroach” movement. The current revolt draws on a long history of student resistance in France. Martin Barnay , writing in New Left Review , traces this history from May 1968 to the high school uprising of 1990, when young people challenged the failures of political authority and helped turn educational grievances into broader social struggles. Today, students are confronting a political establishment that serves the interests of financial elites, the military-industrial complex, and corporate power while dismantling the public institutions and social protections on which working-class and poor communities depend. Jon Henley locates the crisis facing French students within a deeper generational fear that extends far beyond immediate material hardships. He writes: “This generation fears its future will be one of diminishing prospects, poorly paid, unstable jobs, unaffordable living costs and steadily decaying public infrastructure, the end, in short, of the basic socioeconomic security their parents, mostly, enjoyed.” These fears arise from the brutal realities of a capitalist system that has made social abandonment, human suffering, and the disposability of entire generations central to its exercise of economic and political power. Neoliberalism is a cruel and merciless economic, political, and cultural system that has produced staggering inequalities, widespread human suffering, and a relentless assault on democratic life. It operates as a war machine against the social state, dismantling public institutions, concentrating wealth and power in the hands of ruling elites, and creating the conditions in which authoritarianism and fascist politics flourish. Under its rule, democratic values and social obligations are subordinated to the imperatives of privatization, militarization, patriarchy, unchecked self-interest, and the accumulation of wealth and power. Prabhat Patnaik argues that as neoliberalism fails to deliver on its promises of prosperity and loses political legitimacy, ruling elites increasingly embrace neofascist politics, mobilizing racism, ultranationalism, and repression to redirect popular anger away from capitalism and protect their wealth and power. The victims of this savage system include the poor, the working class, women, people of color, immigrants, and especially young people, whose lives and futures are sacrificed to the demands of capital. Yet such brutality also breeds resistance. William Robinson links the suffering inflicted by neoliberalism, from Latin America to the streets of Europe, to a deepening crisis of capitalist legitimacy and the rise of what he calls “the upsurge in popular radical struggles from below.” As neoliberalism's legitimacy crumbles, the uprisings in France and elsewhere expose a struggle that reaches beyond the war on youth to the future of democracy itself . Neoliberalism celebrates the “free possessive individual,” reducing citizenship to consumerism and freedom to the relentless pursuit of private gain. The work of David Harvey and Thomas Piketty exposes how neoliberalism pathologizes the social, destroying the civic bonds and collective responsibilities on which democratic life depends. This assault on the very foundations of solidarity is reinforced by an ideology that, as Stuart Hall warned, portrays the welfare state as “the arch enemy of freedom.” Within this ruthless logic, redistributing wealth, protecting workers, providing public services, and confronting social injustice are condemned as assaults on individual liberty. Corporate power is liberated from democratic accountability, while ordinary people are stripped of the protections and institutions that make freedom meaningful. The ultimate cruelty of this ideology lies in its attempt to convince people that solidarity is a form of tyranny, social responsibility is an assault on freedom, and the pursuit of private wealth is the highest expression of human liberty. Milton Friedman gave this ideology its bluntest expression when he declared that the sole social responsibility of business was to increase its profits. In this worldview, corporate greed becomes a virtue, while the human suffering it produces is dismissed as an acceptable cost of doing business. Wendy Brown warns that neoliberalism is hollowing out democracy, turning its institutions and principles into “ideological shells concealing their opposite” (Chapter 3, p. 52) . This assault reaches beyond elections, civil liberties, and judicial independence. It also targets public education, historical memory, and the critical capacities people need to recognize injustice and resist authoritarian power. When education loses its democratic purpose, society loses one of its most important defenses against the return of fascist politics. The destruction of historical consciousness makes the nightmares of the past easier to normalize and the possibility of collective resistance harder to imagine. Neoliberalism's war on youth reveals the cruelty of a system that destroys the institutions young people need to build meaningful lives while punishing them for resisting their abandonment. Jean and John Comaroff illuminate a central contradiction of global capitalism: young people are celebrated as symbols of the future while increasingly forced to bear the fears, failures, and burdens of the present. As the social state gives way to the punishing state, investments in education, health care, housing, and economic security are sacrificed to corporate wealth and military power. Young people, especially those from poor and working-class communities, are denied the resources necessary to exercise meaningful control over their lives. When they demand justice, their resistance is increasingly met with surveillance, criminalization, and police violence. This is the brutal logic of gangster capitalism: a system that robs young people of their future and then treats their refusal to accept that fate as a threat to be crushed. The French student revolt gives political expression to this struggle, as young people challenge the capitalist forces that have robbed them of economic security, democratic agency, and the right to shape their own future. Related: When Words Become Weapons of Racial Terror 1. France’s Students and the Politics of Abandonment The anger sweeping through French schools has been fueled by years of austerity , overcrowded classrooms, teacher shortages, crumbling buildings, and inadequate educational resources. These conditions fall most heavily on working-class students, particularly those in the impoverished suburbs of Paris, where educational opportunities have been devastated by years of neglect and widening class inequality. For these young people, the destruction of public education is inseparable from the broader assault on their dignity, economic security, and right to a future. Melissa Bell traces the origins of the protests to September 21 at Saint-Exupéry High School in a Parisian suburb, where students joined striking teachers demanding additional staff and educational resources. Although the authorities eventually responded to the immediate demands, the protest had already ignited a much wider movement. Within weeks, demonstrations and school blockades spread across France, drawing hundreds of thousands of students, teachers, and trade union members into the streets. On October 6 alone, the Interior Ministry estimated that approximately 256,000 people demonstrated nationwide, while student organizers placed the number at 450,000. Ellen Francis and Victoria Bisset , writing in The Washington Post , reported that on October 18 “nearly 800,000 people, including students, public workers and others across the country” took part in demonstrations. What began as a local struggle over schooling had become one of France's largest student uprisings in decades. The movement's rapid expansion exposed years of accumulated anger over an education system increasingly unable to meet even the most basic needs of its students. The depth of the crisis becomes especially clear in Bell's account of the conditions facing French students. Despite an increase of approximately 250,000 secondary school students since 2008, France now has fewer secondary school teachers than it did then. More than 70 percent of public-sector classrooms have over thirty pupils, while teacher absences routinely leave students without instruction. Silvana Solano adds further evidence of the systematic neglect of public education. According to figures she cites from the Ministry of National Education, “9.8 percent of secondary teaching hours were left unfulfilled during the previous academic year due to unreplaced teacher absences.” The physical conditions in many schools provide further evidence of this systematic abandonment. Writing in the London Review of Books, Daniella Shrier notes that In some of the most neglected schools in the Paris suburbs, students report infestations of rats and cockroaches, leaking roofs, broken windows, inadequate heating, and toilets without doors. At Collège Georges Politzer in Bagnolet, students complained for months about contaminated tap water before the presence of fecal matter was confirmed. Such conditions reveal the depth of a political order in which the most basic requirements of human dignity are denied to working-class children. Students also report classrooms where temperatures during heat waves reach between 35 and 40 degrees Celsius “rendering learning environments intolerable and hazardous to health.” Many schools also lack sufficient nurses, social workers, and administrative personnel. Such conditions make meaningful education almost impossible, reducing public schools to institutions of managed deprivation rather than spaces in which young people can develop the knowledge, critical capacities, and political agency essential to democratic life. The class character of this educational crisis is especially visible in Seine-Saint-Denis, where Barnay reports that students can lose the equivalent of almost an entire year of schooling because absent teachers are not replaced. Such deprivation reinforces the inequalities that shape their lives long before they enter the classroom. Education becomes another instrument for reproducing class privilege rather than challenging it. The grievances extend beyond deteriorating buildings and missing teachers. Solano (2026) reports that students have also challenged exhausting and poorly organized schedules, the psychological pressures associated with the Parcoursup university admissions system, and the growing uncertainty surrounding their educational and professional futures. Their demands are both specific and far-reaching. They call for the immediate redirection of public resources toward education, the hiring of permanent teachers and substitute personnel, additional nurses and social workers, the renovation of deteriorating school buildings, an end to budget freezes, more reasonable schedules, and fundamental changes to the university admissions system. These demands expose the systematic deprivation of the resources young people need to learn, exercise political agency, and participate in shaping the society they will inherit. Bell draws a revealing contrast with May 1968: while students then famously demanded the impossible, today's protesters insist that they are asking for the bare minimum, an education that allows them to learn. France's spending priorities expose the brutality of these political choices. According to Savage Minds (2026), the proposed 2027 budget would increase military spending by approximately $7.2 billion while allocating only an additional $1.2 billion to education and eliminating 1,588 permanent teaching positions. Students have responded with signs demanding “money for schools, not war.” Their message cuts to the heart of gangster capitalism: the state finds enormous resources for militarism while claiming it cannot afford the teachers, classrooms, and public institutions necessary to sustain a generation's future. Such priorities expose a state willing to finance the machinery of war while starving the institutions that sustain the lives and futures of its young. Related: What I Learned Along the Way: Memory, Education,and the Struggle for the Future 2. From Educational Grievances to a Generational Revolt The revolt against deteriorating schools has become a wider struggle against Macron's austerity policies and the destruction of the social state . Students demanding teachers and decent classrooms are finding common cause with workers, parents, and trade unions confronting the same system of economic exploitation and political abandonment. These emerging alliances carry the possibility of transforming scattered grievances into an organized political struggle against gangster capitalism. Similar currents of revolt are emerging in Spain , where soaring rents and a deepening housing crisis have exposed the cruelty of an economic system that drives working-class families and the elderly into poverty, displacement, and despair, with some facing such desperate circumstances that they have taken their own lives. The growing reach of the revolt is evident in reports by Catherine Porter and Ségolène Le Stradic , who document protests spreading to more than forty French cities, drawing students from working-class suburbs, affluent neighborhoods, prestigious schools, and universities. Parents, teachers, and trade unionists have joined the demonstrations, transforming a revolt over deteriorating schools into a national movement. Their solidarity challenges the class divisions that have long structured educational opportunity in France and brings the defense of public education into a wider struggle against capitalist austerity. What gives this developing movement particular importance is the growing involvement of organized labor. Vračar reports that members of major trade unions, including the General Confederation of Labour (CGT), have joined student demonstrations, in some instances forming protective lines between young protesters and the police. The CGT has emphasized that today's students are tomorrow's workers and should not be forced to bear the consequences of austerity. This recognition opens the possibility of a broader alliance between young people struggling for educational opportunities and workers confronting deteriorating wages, weakened social protections, and growing economic insecurity. The participation of labor unions also provides the student movement with organizational experience, historical memory, and connections to struggles extending far beyond the classroom. Vračar sees in the growing alliance among student organizations, trade unions, and sections of the parliamentary left the possibility of a wider collective movement capable of challenging the government's political and economic priorities. As the revolt expands to confront rising living and fuel costs, attacks on retirement benefits, and “the degrading of public services,” the possibility of a broader movement against capitalist power becomes increasingly concrete. France has a long history of student resistance, with protests over education repeatedly becoming catalysts for wider political upheaval. Barnay recalls how the May 1968 student revolt helped unleash a nationwide strike, while the high school protests of 1990 demonstrated the capacity of young people to challenge political authority. Macron's government now faces the possibility of a convergence des luttes , a coming together of struggles against austerity, declining wages, rising living costs, and the erosion of social protections. The memory of the Yellow Vest movement continues to haunt the political establishment. The prospect of students joining forces with organized labor threatens to turn a revolt over education into a much wider confrontation with capitalist power. The class interests behind Macron's austerity policies are impossible to conceal. Barnay reports that estimates from France's Cour des Comptes indicate that corporate tax cuts and reductions in social-security contributions introduced since 2018 were costing public finances approximately €62 billion annually by 2023. While corporations and the wealthy benefit from these policies, unemployment protections are tightened, the retirement age is raised, and public services are starved of resources. Thomas Piketty exposes the political deception at the heart of this manufactured fiscal crisis, revealing how the language of public debt conceals an extraordinary concentration of private wealth. He writes: To justify the inadequacy of education funding, and in particular the decrease in spending per student, the government and its supporters argue that France cannot afford to invest more. They are making two reasoning errors. Public debt has indeed risen from 20% of GDP in 1970 to 120% today. But at the same time, private wealth has grown much more dramatically: It has gone from 300% to 600% of GDP, with extreme concentration among the wealthiest financial fortunes. In other words, France’s national wealth—the sum of private and public assets minus private and public debts—has never been so high, not only in absolute terms but also as a percentage of GDP (which itself has never been higher). Piketty's analysis lays bare the class politics of austerity. The problem is not a lack of national wealth but its concentration in private hands and the political refusal to redistribute it in the public interest. Public debt becomes a weapon of class power, invoked to justify the destruction of social protections while shielding the enormous fortunes accumulated by ruling elites. This is gangster capitalism at work: a system that protects the fortunes of billionaires while forcing workers, students, and the poor to bear the costs of austerity. The student revolt exposes austerity as a political weapon wielded in the interests of capital, rather than an unavoidable response to economic necessity. The protests in France are also part of a widening international revolt against neoliberal capitalism. Barnay notes that French demonstrators have carried placards invoking Gen Z movements in Nepal, Morocco, and Madagascar. These references suggest a growing recognition among young people that their struggles against austerity, corruption, and political exclusion are connected across national borders. The uprisings in Italy and Albania give further political force to this widening revolt against gangster capitalism. Ana Vračar reports that massive demonstrations in Italy have brought students, teachers, workers, and trade unions into the streets to challenge austerity, the destruction of public education, militarization, and the far-right policies of Giorgia Meloni's government. In Albania, as Democracy Now! reports, students have joined a wider movement against corruption, economic insecurity, deteriorating universities, and the plunder of public resources, including opposition to a planned luxury resort backed by Jared Kushner and Ivanka Trump. In both countries, as in France, these movements have been met with police violence. These revolts expose the accumulated consequences of more than four decades of neoliberal policies that have transferred enormous wealth and power to ruling elites while dismantling the social state and condemning millions, especially young people, to lives of insecurity and dispossession. The political power of these struggles lies in the growing solidarity among students, workers, and educators who are transforming their collective anger into organized resistance against a capitalist system that has robbed them of their dignity, democratic rights, and future. The violence directed against these movements reveals another disturbing feature of the neoliberal order: the growing reliance on the punishing state to crush dissent and protect established power. In India, Prime Minister Narendra Modi's authoritarian government has unleashed a massive police crackdown on young protesters challenging alleged electoral manipulation and the erosion of democratic freedoms. Amnesty International has documented police beatings, demonstrators dragged through the streets, thousands of arbitrary detentions, and restrictions on movement and internet access. What is unfolding in France, Italy, Albania, Spain and India reveals a disturbing international pattern: governments increasingly treat young people demanding justice, dignity, and democratic accountability as enemies of the state. The use of police violence against youth is also a form of political education, designed to teach fear, enforce obedience, and convince an entire generation that challenging established power carries a heavy price. Despite such repression, young people continue to take to the streets, refusing to surrender their political agency or abandon the struggle to overthrow a capitalist system built on exploitation, inequality, and the concentration of wealth and power. Rather than address their grievances, the French government has joined Marine Le Pen and the far right in directing blame toward students and the political left. This convergence in the language of criminalization and repression casts a troubling shadow over the upcoming presidential election, further legitimating the authoritarian politics on which Le Pen has built her political appeal. The courage to resist state violence does not emerge in a historical vacuum. It is shaped by political struggles, collective memories, and educational traditions that teach young people that injustice can be challenged and power held accountable. Will Bunch remarks that French students inherit a political culture shaped by powerful traditions of collective resistance and the defense of democratic rights. Drawing on sociologist Dana R. Fisher, Bunch emphasizes the importance of relationships among students, families, and trade unions in sustaining political protest. French schools also play an important role in keeping these traditions alive. Kitty Sayers notes that students learn from an early age about their country's revolutionary history, the struggles that secured democratic rights, and the obligations of the state to its citizens. The French Revolution and the student revolts of 1968 are part of their education, while classroom debates encourage young people to develop political opinions and defend them. Sayers writes that "The language of rights, citizenship and collective power is woven into French education." Such lessons offer young people a language through which to understand injustice, challenge authority, and recognize protest as a fundamental democratic right. They also help cultivate a sense of solidarity and collective responsibility that challenges the neoliberal celebration of possessive individualism, competition, and the belief that individuals alone are responsible for their fate. In this tradition, democracy is inseparable from the struggle for social rights, public accountability, and the collective power to confront injustice. Sayers also states that French youth, taught to engage as citizens, are more than willing to take to the streets in order to hold power accountable. Through demonstrations, political organizing, and alliances with workers, teachers, and trade unions, French students are putting these lessons into practice. Their resistance demonstrates how historical knowledge and political education can become weapons in the struggle against austerity, state repression, and capitalist domination. Related: Nuremberg’s Warning: When Law Becomes a Weapon Against Democracy 3. The Punishing State and the Criminalization of Youth Resistance The French student revolt carries a warning that extends far beyond the classroom. A generation denied economic security, decent schools, democratic rights, and the possibility of a livable future is refusing to accept its own disposability. These young people are confronting a system of gangster capitalism that concentrates wealth and power in the hands of a ruling elite while treating the needs of the many as expendable. Their revolt exposes the moral and political bankruptcy of a system willing to sacrifice the future of its children to protect the fortunes of the wealthy. The struggle unfolding in France points toward the necessity of overthrowing a capitalist order whose survival depends on exploitation, inequality, and the destruction of the public good. Jean and John Comaroff ’s writings on youth under global capitalism illuminate one of the central contradictions of neoliberal society. They argue that youth embody the deepening contradictions of a society that celebrates them as symbols of the future while denying them the means to build one. Young people are welcomed into the marketplace as consumers, yet increasingly excluded from economic security, meaningful citizenship, and political power. They inherit a world in which the promises of progress have given way to precarious lives, social abandonment, and the destruction of collective responsibility. Their anger becomes politically explosive when they recognize that the system demanding their loyalty is responsible for the destruction of their futures. How a society represents its young reveals much about its political and moral character. Under neoliberal capitalism, young people are celebrated as consumers and symbols of innovation as long as they submit to the demands of the market. When they resist, they become objects of fear, surveillance, and punishment. The political culture of disposability examined in Youth in a Suspect Society: Democracy or Disposability ? increasingly represents young people, especially the poor and racially marginalized, as dangerous populations to be surveilled, disciplined, and controlled. The French government's response to the student revolt exposes the brutality of this machinery of disposability. Young people demanding decent schools and a livable future are confronted with police violence and criminalization. Their refusal to surrender their future becomes grounds for repression, revealing how deeply the punishing state has become an instrument for protecting capitalist power. The political significance of the French student revolt lies in the growing capacity of young people to recognize how their personal hardships are rooted in structures of capitalist exploitation and political domination, organize collectively, and imagine a future beyond the existing order. Through collective struggle, they are breaking with the neoliberal culture of possessive individualism and the belief that capitalism represents the limits of political possibility. Their alliances with teachers, workers, and trade unions point toward the formation of a collective political consciousness capable of transforming anger into organized resistance. In the process, young people are reclaiming their place as historical actors capable of challenging capitalist domination and transforming the conditions of their existence. Pedagogy of Resistance: Against Manufactured Ignorance insists that education is central to the struggle over consciousness, political agency, and the capacity to imagine and fight for a world beyond capitalism. At a time when gangster capitalism has turned ignorance into a political weapon and education into an instrument of conformity and repression, critical pedagogy becomes indispensable to collective resistance. Young people need the historical knowledge, political imagination, and courage to recognize how their private troubles are connected to larger structures of exploitation and domination. They need an education that enables them to question authority, expose the violence of capitalist power, and recognize their capacity to intervene in history. Such an education must become part of a broader struggle to overthrow capitalist power and create a society organized around human needs rather than private profit. The French student revolt has begun to transform a struggle over educational deprivation into a broader confrontation with capitalist domination. Its political significance lies in the recognition that repairing schools, reversing austerity, and restoring social protections, while essential, cannot by themselves dismantle the structures of power responsible for the crisis. What is required is a radical break with a capitalist system that places private profit above human life, legitimates obscene inequalities, and condemns entire generations to lives of insecurity and disposability. The struggle unfolding in France carries the possibility of transforming youthful anger into a mass movement capable of confronting capitalist domination and creating new forms of democratic life. Such a struggle demands critical education, mass political organizing, and solidarities capable of crossing national borders and generations. It also requires a political imagination unwilling to accept the ideological fiction that capitalism represents the end of history. The young people in the streets of France remind us that history remains unfinished and that the existing order is neither natural nor eternal. A society that wages war on its young is waging war on its own future. The students' refusal to accept that fate carries a demand that reaches far beyond France: the overthrow of a capitalist system that has made the disposability of young people a condition of its survival, and the creation of a radically democratic society in which human dignity, economic justice, and the right to a future take precedence over the savage and cruel demands of capital.

articles.title: Adolph Reed on What It Will Take to Defeat Trumpism
articles.author: Adolph Reed
articles.content: With the 2026 midterm elections approaching and Donald Trump’s approval ratings at record lows , it’s easy to hope that we might someday soon find the politics of Trumpism behind us. But it’s far from clear that the Democratic Party can effectively capitalize on anti-Trump sentiment, and Democrats certainly are not offering a clear, compelling program that could address widespread political discontent. In a wide-ranging interview with the European Center for Populism Studies’s Selcuk Gultasli, political scientist and longtime socialist organizer Adolph Reed Jr offers a political-economic interpretation of Trumpism, arguing that the structural contradictions underlying authoritarian nationalism remain fundamentally unresolved. Reed discusses the tensions between capitalist accumulation and democratic legitimacy, challenges race-reductionist explanations of inequality, and critiques neoliberalism’s displacement of class-based politics. Warning that “the threat of another version of Trumpism will continue to be there,” he emphasizes the limitations of left electoral mobilizations without durable working-class organization and advocates for rebuilding a solidaristic, universalist politics capable of confronting both economic inequality and authoritarianism. This transcript has been lightly edited for length and clarity. Selcuk Gultasli Let me begin with how we should conceptualize Trumpism itself. You have recently referred explicitly to the rise of “Trumpist fascism” and elsewhere described Trumpism as the “point of the lance” of a broader fascist international. At the same time, much of the political science literature analyzes Trump through the language of populism , authoritarian populism, or the populist radical right . So, what is obscured when Trumpism is understood primarily as populism rather than as fascism? And what political-economic criteria, in your view, should distinguish fascism from right-wing populism in the contemporary United States? Adolph Reed That’s an important question because a lot of ink has been spilled over a debate that, often enough or all too often, moves the lens away from examining the pragmatic or practical political impacts of the shift and toward a taxonomic exercise, which academics really like to do. From that perspective, I won’t quibble about whether Trump should most properly or most effectively be understood as a fascist, because that automatically opens up a second-order argument about how we delineate the most important features of fascism. I would say two things. One is that Trumpism is clearly a form of authoritarianism , politically. While it’s not necessarily directly coordinated, it seems to be more or less loosely aligned with other variants and expressions of authoritarianism that have been rising across the world, not just in Europe, where it’s most conspicuous, but also now in Latin America. I am concerned about what feels to me like a promiscuous usage of “populism,” and this is another problem that American social scientists often have. Going back to the 2016 presidential campaign, there was a tendency in public intellectual life and all too frequently in political science to define populism in such a way that it would capture any political tendency that’s either somewhat to the right of the conservative coalition or somewhat to the left of the center-left coalition. I found that quite unhelpful and ideological. Trump’s political persona and performance, as well as the performance of his minions, show characteristics or behaviors that make us think of fascism or other authoritarian movements, past and present. But I’m not really hung up on taxonomizing Trumpism. I’m more concerned with trying to make sense of it within the context of contemporary politics and the dangers it poses to us. It feels a little bit like you asked me what time it is and I gave you a disquisition on how to make a watch. I apologize if that’s true. My son says one of our problems, his and mine, is that we tend to speak in paragraphs. Trumpism Beyond Trump Selcuk Gultasli Trumpism is frequently interpreted as a highly personalized movement built around Donald Trump’s charisma, grievances, and domination of the Republican Party. Your analysis, however, places much greater emphasis on the destruction of working-class political capacity, neoliberal hegemony, and the absence of an effective anti-capitalist left. How important is Trump himself to explaining Trumpism? If Trump disappeared from American politics tomorrow, how much of the political formation identified with his name would actually disappear with him? Adolph Reed That’s a very good question because Trump aspires to be a caudillo, or a dictator, in his fantasy life. Unfortunately, for Trump, the distinction between fantasy life and reality is always blurred. So, I don’t know. Partly because Trump insists on surrounding himself with incompetent sycophants, I don’t think the movement, Trumpism, has institutional constituents so much as a gaggle of free-rider billionaires and hustlers who share with him a mean-spirited take on the world in general, along with no shortage of avarice and a propensity for corruption. But I don’t know whether Trumpism per se could survive his demise as a movement. That may be wishful thinking, too. But it is also the case that those forces are still going to be out there. To the extent that they have grounded material interests, those interests aren’t going away. Alliances could potentially develop from the affiliations that have come together under the banner of Trumpism, and they could reorganize. It’s certainly the case that the structural contradictions aren’t going anywhere, especially the increasingly fraught tension between the imperatives of accumulation and political legitimation, principally in neoliberal democracies. We’re also seeing more and more signs that we’ve come to a point at which the Democratic Party is, by default, more generally favored by large capital and governing elites. I have some friends, like Sam Gindin in Canada, who’ve been stressing this point all along. The Democrats provide a certain stability and seem to be better able, at least on the surface, to navigate the tension between the accumulation and legitimation imperatives than Republicans are, although they aren’t particularly successful either. That, as I’ve argued, is one of the factors that led to the rise of Trumpism in the first place. So, in a nutshell, I would say that the structural contradictions that have given space for the rise of authoritarian nationalist, fascist, and populist tendencies around the world remain unresolved. Until those are actually addressed, there will continue to be enough dissatisfaction, desperation, and a sense of undesirable or frightening uncertainty among the general population that, unless there’s some political voice offering a different view of the world and a different strategy for realizing security and well-being, the threat of another version of Trumpism will continue to be there. Economic Insecurity and Status Insecurity Are Not Really Separable Selcuk Gultasli After the 2024 election, you rejected the widespread claim that Trump had assembled a genuinely “new coalition,” arguing that pollsters and political strategists reify demographic categories into supposedly coherent constituencies. How should we therefore interpret shifts toward Trump among segments of black, Latino, immigrant, or working-class voters? Do these shifts reveal an ideological realignment, or do they demonstrate the limitations of treating race, ethnicity, gender, and education as ready-made political blocs? Adolph Reed I’ve argued that those blocs of voters, defined by the pollsters’ ways of aggregating data, are themselves basically artificial. Black male voters under forty . . . what sort of category is that? What does that tell us about any set of individuals and what motivates them? Or Hispanic voters, even Hispanic Catholic voters . . . I think those categories are too idealized and unwieldy to be really useful to us and are more attuned to producing outcomes than to measuring them. That is to say, these formulations of pre-given voting blocs reflect as much an effort to bring those blocs together as meaningful political categories as an effort to help us predict outcomes. They encourage people to understand themselves and their concerns within the taxonomy of those big blocs and act accordingly. I think that’s the first problem. Over the last ten or fifteen years, I’ve become increasingly impressed by how actively the social sciences, or the various disciplines within them, have been more or less willfully making class and political economy disappear from our understanding of American politics, even making the idea of a working class disappear. I don’t count economics and psychology in this. One way to punctuate that last point is to note that, for the two or three decades after World War II in the United States, my discipline, political science, along with sociology and, to a lesser extent, perhaps anthropology, hinged largely on the invention of a middle class as a baseline category in American politics. The middle class is a notion that defies scientific specificity. It’s all over the place. It’s a category that now has to do with attitudes and social position but almost never with one’s place in the political economy. That said, going back to the 2024 election, there seemed to be some loss of support among what are categorized as black or Hispanic constituencies, with some movement from the Democrats to the Republicans. Especially among black voters, the move toward Trump has always been overstated. What the same pollsters are telling us now is that black and Hispanic voters who had flirted with Trump seem to have become disaffected with him. This may seem too tendentious, but I think one of the most meaningful features of this horse-race, postgame handicapping that dominates political interpretation in American life, both in the media and in the academy, is that, consciously or not, it’s more about producing outcomes and constituencies that fit into the abstract categories we’ve made up for them than about understanding what people are actually concerned about. One other point on this: a former colleague of mine, who’s a very smart, insightful, and talented scholar, contended quite militantly after the 2016 election that the bulk of Trump voters were motivated not by economic insecurity but by status insecurity . I thought about that for a minute and wondered: What part of the solar system do you have to live on not to notice that those two aren’t really separable? That just suggests to me, as a critical intellectual historian and a student of the history of ideologies, that there’s some ideology at work in that argument. White Supremacy, Racism, and Historical Explanation Selcuk Gultasli One of your most persistent criticisms of contemporary political analysis is that concepts such as “ white supremacy ” and “racism” are often treated as autonomous causal forces rather than historically specific ideologies embedded in concrete social relations. In your 2020 discussion of socialism and race, you criticized explanations of Trump’s appeal that presume an enduring racial motivation among white workers without sufficient historical or causal specification. How, then, should scholars determine when white supremacy is genuinely explanatory rather than simply descriptive? Adolph Reed I don’t think I have methodological advice to offer. But a big step forward would be to pose the question you’ve raised at every step along the way, at every compass point, and to interrogate the notion of an abstraction. First, what does one mean when one says white supremacy ? Or, for that matter, what does one mean when one says racism ? I’m a pretty historicist scholar, and I’m always conscious that the same phrase can mean radically different things in concrete terms at different historical moments and in different historical contexts. One facet of a perverse strain in liberal intellectual discourse over the last twenty or twenty-five years, which I feel is an American export product in the same way that Air Jordans are but with the heft of foundation money behind it, is the premise that such abstractions as white supremacy or racism, and one could even say sexism, are primordial and, as some sociobiologists would argue, even hardwired or fashioned on the Pleistocene plains or whatever. It seems to me that if we refrain from constructing accounts of the past and its relation to the present that conform to what the sociologist Loïc Wacquant described as the logic of the trial, it might help us jettison an approach to explanation driven by an ideological or moral imperative to demonstrate the existence of racism, whatever we mean by it. Instead, we could start from historical specificity, first trying to root these expressions in their own contexts, to see what they’re responding to and who’s trying to mobilize these ideologies. The sociologist Rogers Brubaker, whose work is very important, has made the point that race, ethnicity, and nationality are all basically different labels for the same phenomenon. But he also notes that we all have multiple ethnic or ethnic-like identities that we experience and carry around all the time. They tend to rise to the conscious mind, or come to the foreground, or retreat into the background in response to cultural and contextual stimuli. For instance, if my postal worker was raised Catholic and I was raised Catholic, then we’re Catholics with each other. Or if someone has family in Cuba and I have family in Cuba, then we’re Cubans together. What’s especially powerful is his argument that ethnic identities, or particular ethnic identities, are likely to come to the foreground when mobilized by political entrepreneurs who want to pursue agendas that require the support of a population substantially larger than the number of people who would benefit concretely from the realization of those agendas. If we think about the fantasized notion of ethnic war, to which people revert to provide evidence for the claim that there are ancient, primordial hatreds, that’s a very good illustration of this. So-called ethnic wars are almost invariably prompted by the actions of self-interested elites. The Lebanese Civil War is a classic case of this. You attack another group, which then retaliates by attacking members of your group. You can then put yourself in the position of telling your group that we, the militia, the ethnically or religiously defined militia, are your only hope for salvation. It’s almost like a mafia extortion racket. So, I’ll draw a line under this by returning to the presumption that there are these primordial identities. To take another illustration, say I have a Polish grandparent and you have a Polish grandparent, and we’re somehow capable of sensing that we share a Polishness. That kind of thinking, like Afro-pessimism and stories of tragic, primordial, intractable ethnic hatreds, is basically the quintessence of what racism is. I’d be happy to be a foot soldier in a campaign to eliminate, or at least counter, that form of thinking, which is best done by trying to organize around a different conception of what shared interests are. Race as Ideology of Ascriptive Hierarchy Selcuk Gultasli You have argued that Marxism’s crucial contribution to understanding race is “demystification”: treating race not as an eternal social substance but as a historically specific ideology that develops within particular relations of production and power. How does this perspective change the way we should understand racial politics under Trump, especially when explicitly racialized rhetoric, immigration politics, and unequal outcomes plainly remain politically consequential? Adolph Reed I’ll tell you one thing: during both of Trump’s presidencies, I’ve said to friends that I’ve occasionally wondered what it would have been like to live through the last decades of the nineteenth century in the American South, not necessarily to have been alive then, but at least to have watched how the wounded Southern planter-merchant capitalist class, weakened by the Populist insurgency from below in the early 1890s, regrouped, self-consciously constructed a white supremacist ideology, imposed it institutionally through the deployment of as much violence, fraud, and intimidation as necessary, and established it as the hegemonic ideology. Because it’s clear that while white supremacists in the Jim Crow–era South were certainly committed to racial hierarchy and the establishment of a racist regime, and I would never challenge the sincerity of that commitment, white supremacy was simultaneously a discourse of mobilization. It helped divide the potential electorate and the forces that had been arrayed against that dominant class, while deploying scapegoating in much the same way that the Trumpists do now. Both things are true. The commitment to a white supremacist ideology was genuine, but it was simultaneously a technique for imposing a dominant order that was skewed toward representing only the interests of the upper class. Both things happen in all these movements. What is most helpful is to see race as a subset of, and I’m often inclined toward the evolutionary metaphor here, a species within a genus of discourses and ideologies of ascriptive hierarchy. That is, taxonomies of hierarchy based on what sets of people, who are themselves partly constructed through the discourse, are by nature rather than what they do. There have been kazillions of these: Christians versus Muslims, for instance, and we could go on with a whole bunch of them. I’ve always found the eugenics era intellectually interesting because the power of this genus of ideologies was so great, for a variety of reasons during that period, that it became basically disconnected even from phenotype. So, you could see the character of constructed ascriptive hierarchy operating a little more clearly. If you look at race that way, it becomes a little easier to see the historical function of different expressions of this ideological genus over time, rather than focusing on just one species. Most People Cannot Imagine a Genuinely Egalitarian Society Selcuk Gultasli In your formulation, contemporary anti-racism can function as “a neoliberal alternative to a Left” when politics becomes centered on proportional representation within existing hierarchies rather than transforming the structures that generate inequality. How would you apply that critique today, when corporations, universities, liberal institutions, and political parties have simultaneously embraced some forms of diversity politics while economic inequality has remained deeply entrenched? Where is the boundary between necessary opposition to racism and what you regard as race-reductionist politics? Adolph Reed There’s a lot of undoing that needs to be done, unfortunately. There’s a much more complex account to be given of the disappearance of a left grounded in a political-economic understanding of inequality. But we all know it’s happened. It’s happened even within social democratic parties in Europe, where those traditions have always been stronger than their counterparts in the United States. There was a brief period when I was fairly close to Die Linke through a North American left dialogue, and it was possible to see, even then, a tendency within that movement toward a division between what could be summarized as a class-based left and an identity-based left. Frankly, the victory of what we understand as neoliberalism helped establish the hegemony of a notion of actionable inequality that comes down to disparities or disparate outcomes and the dynamics and practices that produce those outcomes among ascriptively defined groups. This is essentially about their ability to participate in, or take advantage of, equal opportunity under capitalism. We’ve now reached a point where capitalist class rule is so dominant that it’s not even possible for most people to imagine a genuinely egalitarian way of organizing society that’s actually different from what currently exists. I don’t know why I’m trying to be quiet about this, but that’s what I think the ultimate problem is. But if you’ll pardon the plug, an online academic journal I’m associated with, nonsite.org , is publishing a three-part symposium called Capitalism 1996–2026 . The first installment came out [earlier in October], and I strongly encourage all your readers and listeners to take a look at it. There are four really strong articles. Racial Wealth? Selcuk Gultasli Your work with Merlin Chowkwanyun criticizes a discourse of racial disparity that carefully documents unequal outcomes but can leave their causal mechanisms underspecified. In the current political environment, how should researchers analyze racial disparities in wealth, health, policing, education, or incarceration without either minimizing racism or converting statistical disparities themselves into proof of a singular racial cause? Adolph Reed The first step is always to interrogate whether what seems like a racial disparity is, in fact, a racial disparity. Because it could simply be a statistical artifact that conceals other dynamics producing the apparent unequal outcome, which don’t necessarily have anything to do with race. In the COVID-19 case, for instance, what initially appeared to be massive racial differences in both incidence and morbidity became much more clearly attributable to environmental factors as time went on and more data came in. These included the jobs people have, where they live, the transportation they depend on, and underlying tendencies or morbidity factors. These factors may be racial to the extent that a history of inequality positions some groups as structurally, on average, more vulnerable than others. But part of our argument was to question what we gain, even in areas like health and criminal justice, including police killings, by defining these outcomes as definitively caused by racial disparity. The typical approach begins by identifying evidence of racial disparity, which often requires goosing the data, as it were, or inflecting its interpretation toward race as an abstraction. This also functions to justify the abstract claim that racism is a political force that needs to be dealt with. But there’s no causal mechanism there. That’s part of the problem. I also find the emergence of the racial wealth gap as another significant part of this discourse especially fascinating. First of all, roughly 70 to 75 percent of so-called white wealth is controlled by the richest 10 percent of white people. Between 70 and 75 percent of so-called black or Hispanic wealth is also controlled by the richest 10 percent of black and Hispanic people. So, what does racial wealth mean in this context? I’ve said in talks and in my classes that we’re ideologically predisposed to believe, at least in the United States, that all black people think with one brain and share every aspiration, and therefore what’s good for any one black person is ipso facto good for all black people, for one tortured reason or another. I suggest stepping outside that predisposition. Let’s assume a white female nurse loses her job, has no independent source of funds, and is on the verge of being evicted from her apartment. Where is the pot of white wealth she gets to go to? Where is the teacup, presumably, from which she can get her rent money? When you think of it that way, the idea of racial wealth seems all the more preposterous. So, I’d say there is no such thing as black wealth, white wealth, or any other group wealth. To that extent, there can’t be a racial wealth gap. My good friend and colleague Walter Benn Michaels and I started saying, even before we knew each other and quite independently of each other, that when you hear the word “race,” you should think “unicorn,” because race is as real as unicorns are. Just as you can taxonomize races, you can taxonomize unicorns in any way you want, because you’re not really constrained by having to approximate the empirical reality of the unicorn. Race is the same way. Let’s get that mixed-up stuff straight.
