Universalism, Anti-Discrimination, and Working-Class Solidarity Selcuk Gultasli Your work repeatedly returns to the possibility of solidaristic, universalist politics organized around shared material interests. Critics of this approach often argue that universal programs can reproduce racial inequalities unless they are explicitly designed around historically specific forms of disadvantage. How would you answer that objection? What would a genuinely multiracial, democratic socialist universalism look like institutionally rather than rhetorically? Adolph Reed It seems to me, frankly, that this argument is a red herring. It’s simply a matter of committing to conscious and active anti-discrimination within the framework of universalist politics. The presumption of essential solidarity is what provides the basis for challenging prejudice, which is, after all, an attitude, as well as discriminatory practices. So, I think it’s a nonissue. It’s a smoke screen, much like the idea that there are people out there called class-first Marxists or whatever. No Social Transformation Without an Organizational Base Selcuk Gultasli The Bernie Sanders campaigns appeared, briefly, to revive mass interest in democratic socialism and decommodified public goods such as universal health care and free higher education. Yet the organizational breakthrough many supporters anticipated did not follow. Was Sanders primarily evidence that a latent constituency for social democracy exists in the United States, or did the movement around him reveal how weak the organizational infrastructure necessary for democratic socialism has become? Adolph Reed I think both things are true. In the spirit of full disclosure, I worked on both Sanders campaigns. Also, much of the Sanders program actually came straight from the Labor Party in the United States, founded in 1996, in which I was also deeply involved. Very few people believed that Sanders actually had a chance to win either nomination, though some of us thought that if he could somehow win the nomination, he would have a better chance of winning the presidency than Hillary Clinton did. We’ll never know. But many of us also thought it was really just as well that he didn’t win the presidency, because you can’t elect your way to social transformation, at least not without an organizational base. What we thought the campaigns could do, both times, was publicly dramatize the problem of intensifying inequality and insecurity in the United States, show that it was possible to imagine confronting those problems, and stimulate institutionally grounded organizing that could generate another political formation capable of pushing the struggle forward. But I was disappointed. During the first campaign, seven unions formed a Labor for Bernie group, and they acted in solidarity and coherently throughout the campaign. Interestingly, most of those unions had also been part of the Labor Party twenty years earlier. But for various reasons, some of which had to do with the debasement of American politics already underway, we came out of the 2016 presidential election and went straight into state elections, which were crucial to the unions’ concerns. So, the momentum generated through Bernie’s first campaign dissipated into politics as usual among the left trade unions. That’s one sense in which I say both of the possibilities you mentioned were correct. Something similar happened the second time. We were a little closer to gaining traction after 2020. Then COVID hit, and the country immediately went into lockdown. I’d been working in South Carolina with my colleagues, trying to build on a grassroots base in support of single-payer healthcare, Medicare for All, on which we’d made a lot of headway during the campaign, notwithstanding the fact that Sanders was badly beaten in the primary. COVID tended to undercut those efforts. But I’ll say this: I work with the Debs-Jones-Douglass Institute, a nonprofit we created with the Labor Party to undertake worker education, political education, cultural activities, and research on behalf of working-class politics. We’ve been doing this since the early 1990s, and the materials we produced in the 1990s, just a few years after the end of the Cold War, had to tiptoe around even using the word capitalism or being at all critical of it. That environment has changed radically. I even had to apologize to my undergraduate students for a course I’m teaching this semester because it didn’t assume they were as attuned to criticisms of capitalism as they actually were. The majority of the students in this class are just second-year college students, albeit precocious ones. One of the quips in the labor movement is that often the best organizer you have is the boss. That’s the case here. Thirty more years of going down the neoliberal road, especially since 2008, have made working people in general more skeptical and more open to critiques that begin by explaining how capitalism works and how those processes are connected to their insecurity. Walking on Two Legs Selcuk Gultasli Finally, you have argued that there is “no effective substitute for an anti-capitalist left” and that confronting the far right requires the patient construction of a real working-class constituency rather than episodic mobilization around elections. Whatever happens on November 3, what should democratic socialists, trade unionists, and the broader left actually do the morning after the midterms? What would count, over the next five or ten years, as evidence that an organized political force capable of contesting both neoliberalism and the far right is genuinely being built? Adolph Reed I have a pat answer to that: the same thing they did the morning before the election. Let me offer an illustration. During the 2020 campaign, the Sanders campaign sent me on a labor tour of South Carolina. South Carolina is probably the most reactionary state in America, though that changes from day to day, and perhaps often has the lowest trade union density in the entire country. One of my stops was at a steelworkers’ union hall in Georgetown, South Carolina, on the coast. Among those in attendance were a couple of white rank-and-file members who had come to the hall on either a Saturday or Sunday morning. One of them was a younger guy, maybe forty at most. He volunteered that he liked the Sanders economic program but couldn’t understand why the Democrats kept getting bogged down in what he called moral issues. We had a little back-and-forth about what he meant, and it turned out he was referring to same-sex marriage and abortion. I was there as a supplicant, so I wasn’t going to be combative with him in any way. I tried a number of soft-pedaling approaches, like “Live and let live” or whatever, but nothing worked. Finally, I asked, what’s more important to you? Having a good, secure job, good wages, benefits, access to desirable housing, adequate health care, the ability to provide your kids with a good education, and the opportunity to go back to school if you want? Or ensuring that no two people of the same sex can ever marry and that no woman can ever end an unwanted pregnancy? No, that didn’t convert him, but I didn’t expect it to, because I was just some fast-talking clown from Philadelphia. But it stopped him in his tracks for a few seconds. I couldn’t help thinking: What if I were his brother-in-law, his kids’ soccer coach, his neighbor, or a coworker on his shift, someone who had some standing in his eyes and could have this conversation with him repeatedly over time? No, I don’t think the ideal outcome would necessarily be for him to become a militant advocate of reproductive rights. But at least over time and on the basis of solidarity, he could come to accept that other people have different ways of seeing these issues, even though they’re committed to the same fundamental program of transforming society in the interests of working people. That’s where real tolerance of difference could come from. You only get that through building a solidaristic movement over time. We haven’t had anything like that in the United States, at least during my adult life. In fact, for most of my adult life, we haven’t even had the benefit of direct connections to people who knew it was possible to have a world like that and who had fought for that solidarity, both inside and outside the trade unions, in the period before World War II. I may be old-fashioned, but I just don’t see any other way to do it. There’s no other way to get there. Now, that’s not to say that you shouldn’t pay attention to elections at all. I vote in every election. There’s a phrase the Maoists used to use a long time ago: walking on two legs. You’ve got to be able to focus both on what needs to be done to stop the bleeding right now, to keep things from getting worse, and on where we’re trying to go in the long run. That’s my argument for everybody. This article originally appeared in Jacobin , a democratic socialist magazine publishing long-form essays and analysis on politics, economics, and culture. articles.title: Israel’s Election Offers a Bleak Future for the Palestinians
articles.author: Ambra Suriano
articles.content: Israel’s parliamentary elections are fast approaching on October 27, with Benjamin Netanyahu facing a challenge from the opposition leader Gadi Eisenkot. Netanyahu is backed by a coalition of religious ultranationalist parties, while Eisenkot advocates a more liberal or secular form of Zionism, pledging to achieve what his party describes as a Zionist goal: “to make Israel, by 2048, a prosperous model state — a source of pride, built on partnership, fellowship and mutual responsibility.” But what would a victory for either bloc mean for Palestinian society in the West Bank and the Gaza Strip? Unfortunately, whoever wins the election, there is not going to be any change to Israel’s denial of basic rights to the Palestinian people. Whatever else may divide them, the two rival coalitions share common ground in their staunch opposition to a Palestinian state and their insistence that Israel’s security must be further strengthened. A Democracy for the Jews Since its establishment, Israel has defined itself as a democratic state surrounded by enemies and fighting for its survival. However, while Israel has extended rights of citizenship and political participation to Jewish immigrants, Palestinians who already lived on the land have been subjected to mass displacement and denied equivalent rights under Israeli rule. Since 1967, Israeli governments have maintained a military occupation of the West Bank and the Gaza Strip. This has effectively created a single territorial space under Israeli control, in which Jewish Israelis enjoy the full rights of citizenship, while Palestinians remain subject to military occupation and its extensive restrictions. Israel has advanced the de facto annexation of Palestinian territory through colonial practices of occupation. Its consequences are stark: the creation of a blockade that Human Rights Watch recognized as a crime against humanity in a 2024 report; the perpetuation of daily violence by approximately 730,000 Israeli settlers living as full citizens of Israel in the West Bank; the systematic restriction of Palestinian freedom through the establishment of hundreds of checkpoints, road blocks, and other barriers. Israeli leaders have long justified the colonization of Palestinian territory and the systematic oppression of the Palestinian people by reference to two overlapping narratives: the need to securitize the state and the religious imperative to establish Israeli sovereignty over Palestinian land they regard as part of the biblical inheritance of the Jewish people. While much of the Israeli left and center has traditionally favored the first rationale, the Israeli right embraces both, openly advocating the annexation of Palestinian territory. The election of Netanyahu’s government in December 2022, on a platform explicitly supporting annexation, illustrates the extent of domestic support for the occupation among Israeli voters. However, Gadi Eskenot has accused Netanyahu and his allies of failing to achieve its stated goal of ensuring Israel’s security since October 2023: “Three years on, and the war’s objectives have still not been achieved. Hamas, Hezbollah and Iran are already preparing for the next round.” The political program put forward by the opposition does not address the near-total destruction of Gaza’s social, economic, and political fabric, or the accusations of genocide brought against Israel before the International Court of Justice. Still less does it offer a path toward realizing the Palestinian people’s right to self-determination. As Eisenkot stressed in August this year: “There is no Palestinian state, and no Palestinian state will be established under the government we form.” In fact, once again echoing a long-standing pattern in Israeli politics, the opposition’s electoral platform centers on national security. It pledges to “develop and implement a new national security doctrine,” strengthen the Israel Defense Forces (IDF), reinforce security along the borders — without specifying which borders — and turn Israel into a regional power while enhancing its standing on the world stage. The most significant proposed departure, however, lies in the commitment to integrate “ultra-Orthodox and Arab communities” into the IDF. The contest between the two coalitions in the upcoming elections is a contest between political forces that offer no prospect of change in the approach to the Palestinian question, reflecting widespread indifference among the Israeli public toward the plight of the Palestinians. This is further illustrated by the categorical rejection by representatives of eight parties — Likud, Yashar, B’Yachad, Religious Zionist, Reservists-Economic Party, Yisrael Beiteinu, Otzma Yehudit, and Amcha Yisrael — of the idea that a Palestinian state should exist. The responses range from “hell no” to “we’ll fight it . . . it’s wrong, it’s stupid, it’s against God, and it’s dangerous.” Yet the persistent emphasis of the candidates on the need for security suggests that a pervasive sense of anxiety and fear exists within Israeli society, even as Israel continues to deploy extensive military force in Gaza, killing large numbers of civilians. In turn, this sense of fear provides political elites with fertile ground for mobilizing public support. A striking manifestation of this is the continued tendency to sacralize military power. The Smiling Soldiers Project , launched in the aftermath of October 7, illustrates this tendency, portraying soldiers as united by a spirit of brotherhood. The inclusion of soldiers’ photographs on social media pages devoted to Israeli culture, such as “Israel Picture,” similarly reflects the prominent place that the military occupies in the country’s national imaginary. The Politics of Fear The sense of vulnerability among Israeli citizens has provided political elites across the spectrum with fertile ground upon which to construct a rhetoric of fear, amplifying public anxieties to mobilize support for political and economic interests. Menachem Begin, prime minister of Israel from 1977 to 1983, offered a typical example of such rhetoric in 1968: “The enemies of the Jewish state, who surround it on every side, are plotting to destroy the returnees to Zion, the survivors of the German campaign of extermination.” We can find the same kind of language being used today. In September, Netanyahu’s Finance Minister Bezalel Smotrich described Gaza’s two million Palestinians as “2 million Nazis,” claiming that generations had been raised to harbor a deeply antisemitic hatred of Israel. Statements of this kind tap into collective anxieties and channel them into support for practices of oppression that are framed as inevitable and fundamentally necessary. In doing so, they deflect responsibility for Israel’s conduct and cast the state as the sole victim of the conflict. A particularly striking visual expression of this dynamic came in a 2013 poster produced by StandWithUs, an international organization that describes its mission as defending “the civil and human rights of those who align with our mission of supporting Israel.” The poster juxtaposed Israeli soldiers with images of concentration camp prisoners. The montage drew on the collective memory of the Holocaust to frame Israeli soldiers as harmless victims and Israel’s security concerns as the outcome of an existential threat hanging over the state. As the electoral platforms of the two main contenders demonstrate, the Palestinian right to self-determination does not feature in the political vision being presented to Israeli voters. While Netanyahu insists that continuing the wars launched under his premiership is essential to strengthening Israel’s security, Eisenkot promises to introduce new reforms to the country’s security and military establishment. He does so without spelling out how he would address the devastation in Gaza, settler violence in the West Bank and southern Lebanon, or the war with Iran. In The Wretched of the Earth , Frantz Fanon argued that colonialism not only deforms the lives of the colonized; it also transforms the minds of those who sustain it. The violence of colonialism, together with the anger and fear that violence naturally produces, reaches beyond its immediate victims, reshaping the political imagination of the society that perpetrates it. Such dramatic dynamics have extensive psychological and, consequently, social and political reverberations. On the one hand, they leave the Palestinians no choice other than living without human, let alone political, rights. At the same time, they breed racism and trauma within Israeli society, fueling intolerance and a relentless pursuit of security that erodes democratic pluralism within Israel’s own Jewish-majority democracy. This is evident, for instance, in the assaults on freedom of speech in Israel over the last two decades, in demonstrations targeting Palestinian citizens of Israel, where marchers have chanted “Death to the Arabs,” and in government threats to revoke the citizenship of the Israeli filmmakers of NAZA , a documentary featuring interviews with soldiers who have served in the war over Gaza in recent years. Colonial domination does not leave the colonizer untouched. The colonizer may conquer the land, but, in turn, colonialism also conquers the mind. articles.title: When Gas Diplomacy Sounds Like Regime Change
articles.author: Christos Avramidis
articles.content: “We can do this to any country we want. We can do it here too.” According to a Wall Street Journal investigation published on September 25, Kimberly Guilfoyle, Donald Trump’s ambassador to Greece, conveyed this message during a March dinner in Athens while discussing the expected fall of the Romanian government with Greek Minister for the Environment and Energy Stavros Papastavrou. Papastavrou replied that the United States could not replace a Greek government elected by the Greek people. Although Guilfoyle’s lawyer disputes the newspaper’s description of the exchange, the report immediately caused political controversy in both Greece and Romania. In Greece, the alleged words landed on particularly sensitive ground. They sounded less like an eccentric diplomatic indiscretion than an updated, Trumpian version of a much older doctrine through which Washington decides how much sovereignty smaller countries are allowed to exercise. The story has since taken another turn. On October 13, the White House asked Guilfoyle to resign amid a widening series of misconduct allegations, all of which she denies. These went well beyond the reported conversation about governments in Greece and Romania and included allegations involving gifts and favors, the use of official access, contacts with Greek business interests and lobbyists, and her conduct in office. Yet the allegations surrounding Guilfoyle’s departure are only one part of the story. Her own account of what she believed she had accomplished in Greece points to the broader political and economic project behind her tenure. Her farewell statement deserves credit for its candor about the political economy of her mission. Guilfoyle said she had worked to deliver “meaningful victories for the American people.” She pointed to expanded US liquefied natural gas (LNG) exports through the Vertical Corridor, new opportunities for American businesses and investment, stronger “American energy dominance,” and a United States that remains the “indispensable leader in Southeast Europe.” The beneficiaries she chose to name were not Greek households struggling with energy bills but the American people, American businesses, and American geopolitical power. The latest scandal was not Guilfoyle’s first collision with Greek public opinion. Her relationship with the country had started badly before she even took up the post. During the 2015 debt crisis, after Greek voters rejected a new austerity package, Guilfoyle called Greeks “freeloaders” on Fox News and told them to “suck it up.” She also complained that they retired too early and compared the need to discipline them to training a dog that urinates on a rug. The comments resurfaced when Trump nominated her for the Athens post and provoked sharp criticism in Greece. Guilfoyle subsequently stressed her “love and admiration” for Greece in public but issued no retraction or apology for the original remarks. The Business Behind the Scandal The Wall Street Journal investigation is fundamentally a story about energy, business, and lobbying. At its center is Christos Marafatsos, a registered lobbyist for AKTOR Group, one of Greece’s largest construction and infrastructure companies. According to the Wall Street Journal and federal lobbying records cited by the House Foreign Affairs Committee, AKTOR paid Marafatsos $160,000 through June 2026 to establish contacts with the Department of State, Department of Energy, and the Executive Office of the President. He accompanied Guilfoyle to official meetings, where some participants reportedly assumed that he was part of her staff. Guilfoyle has simultaneously been one of the most visible advocates of expanding American LNG exports through Greece and across Southeast Europe. AKTOR has positioned itself to benefit heavily from that expansion. Through Atlantic SEE LNG Trade, a joint venture with the state-owned Public Gas Corporation of Greece (DEPA), the company has signed long-term deals around the import and transport of US LNG through the Vertical Corridor. Beginning in 2030, the venture is contracted to buy at least one million metric tons of American LNG every year for twenty years under its expanded agreement with Venture Global. AKTOR’s own projections demonstrate the scale of the opportunity. The company says LNG agreements already signed or in development could eventually generate around €90 million in annual EBITDA (earnings before interest, taxes, depreciation, and amortization) from 2030, or around €1.8 billion over twenty years. These are company projections, not guaranteed profits. But they make clear why the emerging gas route is not simply a matter of abstract geopolitics. The Vertical Gas Corridor is supposed to move gas from Greek LNG terminals north through Bulgaria and Romania toward Moldova, Ukraine, and Central Europe. Washington and European governments present the project as one that will advance “energy security” and diversification from Russian gas. But replacing one form of dependence with another is not the same as independence. Europe’s growing reliance on LNG ties prices more closely to global gas markets, competition with Asian buyers, shipping constraints, and geopolitical shocks. The European Commission itself notes that gas remains a key price-setting fuel in Europe’s electricity system, while LNG has become far more important to the continent’s supply mix. The environmental bill will also be substantial. LNG is not simply pipeline gas arriving on a ship. Gas must be extracted, processed, liquefied at extremely low temperatures, shipped across an ocean, and converted back into gas before it can even be burned. The International Energy Agency finds that, on average, LNG has substantially higher supply-chain emissions than natural gas produced close to where it is consumed, largely because of the additional energy required for liquefaction and long-distance shipping. The Price Is Set by the Most Expensive Tomato The cost-of-living problem does not begin or end with LNG. It is also embedded in the architecture of the European electricity market, and in Greece’s implementation of the EU Target Model through the Hellenic Energy Exchange. The simplest way to explain marginal pricing is with a market stall. Imagine filling a basket with tomatoes from several sellers. Most stalls offer them cheaply, but demand is high enough that you also need tomatoes from one expensive stall. Now imagine that the rules require you to buy every tomato in the basket at the price charged by that last, most expensive stall. That is how the electricity market works in Europe. There are some complications to the overall picture: retail bills also reflect contracts, hedging, network charges, taxes, and state support. But the wholesale mechanism matters enormously. According to the European Commission, gas supplied only around 17.6 percent of EU electricity generation in 2025. Yet fossil fuel plants still determined electricity prices in roughly half of all hours across the EU. The EU itself acknowledged this problem during the energy crisis. Emergency legislation recognized that exceptionally high gas prices could generate extraordinary revenues for lower-cost electricity producers and temporarily imposed a revenue cap on some inframarginal generators. Motor Oil reported €689 million in group earnings after tax in the first half of 2026, compared with €163 million in the same period of 2025 and €362 million in the first half of 2024. Its first-half profits were therefore more than four times their 2025 level and around 90 percent higher than two years earlier. HELLENiQ ENERGY shows a similar pattern using its own adjusted measure. Adjusted net income reached €393 million in the first half of 2026, compared with €128 million in 2025 and €236 million in 2024. This means adjusted profits more than tripled in a year. The two companies use different accounting measures, so the figures should not simply be added together. But the comparison with their own recent results makes the trend difficult to miss. Nor did all these profits come from the Greek domestic market. A substantial share of refining activity is export-oriented. That distinction matters. But it does not exhaust the policy choices available to the Greek government. Poland has enacted a temporary windfall tax on extraordinary fuel sector profits, with a 60 percent rate on profits above the statutory benchmark and advance payments during the year. Greece could have pursued a similar extraordinary tax. It did not. The government could also have imposed a profit margin cap at refinery level. It did not do that either. We can see the consequences in Greece today: households confront intense pressure from energy costs while the country’s dominant refining groups have recorded a sharp rebound in profitability. Rubio in Athens Marco Rubio’s visit to Athens in October supplied an almost theatrical coda to the controversy. For the day of his official meetings, Greek police imposed a twenty-four-hour ban on all outdoor public gatherings in a broad section of central Athens surrounding the US Embassy. The official order justified the measure on public security grounds and warned of the risk of serious crimes and disruption to social and economic life. On the eve of the visit, thousands of workers, trade unionists, university and school students, and left-wing organizations marched through central Athens against US policy and Greece’s involvement in war. Police blocked the main demonstration from reaching the US Embassy. But in a surprise action, trade unionists reached a point opposite the embassy, unfurled banners, and lit flares, making their protest visible despite the security cordon. The World Federation of Trade Unions reported that police repeatedly attempted to block demonstrators and used tear gas. A visit devoted to deepening the “strategic” relationship with Washington took place amid restrictions on public protest. It was challenged in the streets by social forces contesting the economic and geopolitical costs of that relationship. For Greek audiences, both the Guilfoyle affair and Rubio’s visit carried echoes of a much longer history of US intervention. During the Greek Civil War, Washington became the principal external backer of the Greek government and the anti-communist monarchical order, supplying weapons, aircraft, and military advisers. Greece also became one of the first postwar battlefields where American-made napalm was used against the communist-led Democratic Army, years before the weapon became notorious in Vietnam. In 1965, the US Embassy concluded that the United States should, if possible without open confrontation, prevent the ousted, democratically elected Prime Minister Georgios Papandreou from returning to power. After the colonels seized power in April 1967, Washington stopped short of a rupture with the junta and continued substantial military assistance. Even Bill Clinton acknowledged, during his 1999 visit to Athens, that the United States had allowed its Cold War interests to prevail over its obligation to support democracy. The Same Corridor Arguments on the European left have sometimes treated anti-imperialism and everyday class politics as if they belonged to separate universes. One involves the North Atlantic Treaty Organization, military bases, diplomacy, and sovereignty, while the other involves wages, rent, heating, and food. The Vertical Corridor and the EU electricity market show how artificial that separation can be. A single policy complex can expand American geopolitical leverage and create decades of revenue for US LNG exporters while generating major returns for Greek capital and deepening Southeast Europe’s dependence on fossil fuel infrastructure. At the same time, it can expose households to a market in which expensive gas sets the wholesale price of electricity that is generated much more cheaply from other sources. Guilfoyle’s alleged remarks about Washington’s power were only one part of a much broader series of controversies surrounding her tenure. By the time the White House asked her to resign, scrutiny extended far beyond that conversation. But behind the individual scandals lie contracts, lobbyists, terminals, pipelines, corporations, and billions of euros. The democratic question and the cost-of-living question are not competing stories. They run through the same corridor. articles.title: Natural Progress and the Gilded Age: A Review of Our Kindred Creatures
articles.author: Rochester Red Star: News from Rochester DSA
articles.content: by Travis Covitz Combining my long-standing interest in animal welfare with Gilded Age politics, Our Kindred Creatures: How Americans Came to Feel the Way They Do About Animals by Bill Wasik and Monica Murphy caught my eye at the local library. This 2024 book explores the rise of the American animal welfare movement from the 1860s through the 1890s, looking at pets, livestock, scientific research, wildlife, circuses, and more. Although I was frequently underwhelmed with the politics of the authors, I found this book quite thought-provoking. It is absolutely true that the relationship between the average American and different animals has completely transformed in the past 150 years. Anybody who wants to achieve social change should learn how this came to be. Today the street is considered the place of the car, but it has not always been that way. Our Kindred Creatures starts by asking us to turn back time to the birth of the American industrial city, where the street was shared by man and beast. Stray cats and dogs ran loose, covered in fleas and acting as a constant threat of rabies. Cattle, swine, and more were herded from the farms where they were raised to the butchers who processed them. Horses were, well, the workhorses, moving people, goods, and equipment across the city. Individual acts of cruelty and violence were the norm, not the exception, and Enlightenment philosophy decreed that these animals were unfeeling automatons. To tell the story of American animal welfare, the authors follow three main “heroes” of the movement. All three were white elites in New England. However, rather than leaning into the individualist narrative of social change, the authors consistently demonstrate that these people did not act alone, but used their influential, organized relationships to achieve widely-felt change. The structure of focusing on these three activists serves, rather, to compare and contrast their different tactics in the cause of animal welfare. Henry Bergh was a ‘vigilante’ who used lawfare to protect animals, George Angell was an ‘educator’ who fostered social clubs and magazines for animal welfarists to come together and share ideas, and Caroline White was an ‘innovator’ who helped establish the first animal shelter. Wasik and Murphy highlight the uniting feature of Romantic philosophy, and the other forms of activism these individuals took part in. White was involved in the suffragist movement and Angell became an anti-war advocate. The authors argue that the animal welfare movement came to be as a way for white elites to focus their good will after the success of abolition. The authors themselves relied frequently on emotional appeals and vivid imagery to get their point across. I generally fall pretty evenly on the need for balance between emotion and reason, so I am not inherently opposed to emotion in a political argument, but it did frequently make me so activated that I had to put the book down. Wasik and Murphy clearly have a lot more experience with archives than with animals. They meander between animal welfare and animal rights, in a way that is unclear whether they are staying wholly committed to the Gilded Age context, or they are just that out of touch with modern animal use philosophy. Occasional leaps from the Gilded Age to today feel forced and politicized, rather than a genuine attempt to synthesize history. A phenomenon that I found quite interesting was the way in which anti-welfare politicians made use of the contradictions in animal welfare elitism. For example, labor rights were consistently pitted against the advancement of animal welfare, and some animal welfare legislation was fought specifically on the grounds that it would discriminate against immigrants. Animal welfarists also had a troubled relationship with paternalism and frontier colonialism. The whole concept of animal welfare is, arguably, paternalist in nature, ‘providing a voice for those without one’. Gilded Age animal welfarists who lamented the extinction of the bison saw it as an inevitable part of the march of progress – just as Manifest Destiny was inevitable – and the establishment of national parks, like Yellowstone, were acts of displacing indigenous nations. Wasik and Murphy do try to push back on this paternalism as a mis-step, but they themselves occasionally fall into the trap of valorizing animal ‘innocence’ over human ‘sin’. Despite the difficulties I had with some of the choices of the authors, I did really appreciate how this book sketched out Gilded Age activism. Seeing the way that clashes between Enlightenment ideals and Romanticism, the changing role of religion, and different ideas of ‘progress’ informed what was possible for changemakers was informative and allowed me to think more deeply about our own moment of social upheaval. I do not think this book is especially helpful for someone trying to learn about the animal industry, but it is a great read for someone wanting to learn more about Gilded Age politics.
