articles.title: UAW Members at Triumph Group Vote 99% to Authorize Strike
articles.author: Justin Mayhugh
articles.content: After a two-day vote, UAW Local 405 members at Triumph Group who make engine controls and other components for U.S. military aircrafts voted 99% (148-1 with 86% turning out) in favor of authorizing a strike for any time after the current union contract expires at midnight on October 31. Core demands include sectoral standard wages, job security, cost-of-living protection, affordable healthcare and no concessions, among other priority issues the company has not even attempted to meet the bargaining committee on. “This vote should send a clear message to Triumph Group that UAW Local 405 members are not settling for their abysmal proposals,” said UAW Region 9A Director Brandon Mancilla. “During the life of our last contract, Triumph Group made $680 million off the work of these members. Our members in West Hartford are no different than UAW aerospace workers across the country. Triumph can afford to do better and this vote is a sign that they must put a better offer forward.” In addition to $687 million in profits over the same five-year duration as the term of the current union contract, Triumph’s CEO was paid $31.7 million – for a total of $61.6 million total paid to the CEO in the last decade. Right now, new hires at Triumph are paid $25.25 per hour. The average wage for a Triumph worker is $39.34, with no cost-of-living adjustment (COLA) to protect against historic inflation. Meanwhile, the production and assembly rates for UAW members at Rolls Royce and GE Aerospace are $43.70 and $43.79, respectively, and they have cost-of-living protections. “It was just hours before our strike vote that the company finally gave us an economic proposal – 8 days before our contract expiration,” said UAW Local 405 President Benjamin Wilcox. “Frankly, the company is still not taking our membership seriously. Here’s hoping the results of this strike vote helps convince them just how different we are doing things this year.” UAW Local 405 represents 174 members at Triumph Group in West Hartford, CT, where they perform highly skilled manufacturing, machining, assembly, and technical work supporting the aerospace industry. These UAW members contribute to the production, repair, and overhaul of critical U.S. military aircraft components and systems, meeting the highest standards of quality, safety, and reliability.

articles.title: Political Revolt in California
articles.author: Zoë Meyers
articles.content: The opinions expressed here are solely the author's and do not reflect the opinions or beliefs of the LA Progressive. Retired probation officer Diana Salcedo had downsized to a home in Imperial’s Paseo del Sol neighborhood and was looking forward to a new chapter in her life caring for her mother and young grandchildren. Then Salcedo found out about a proposal to build what could be California’s largest data center across the street. The more she learned about how data centers affect energy, water and quality of life for those living nearby, the more upset she became. “I was so angry,” she said. “I even cried.” That outrage inspired Salcedo, 65, a Republican who supports President Donald Trump, to join a grassroots movement of local residents fighting the proposed Imperial Valley Computer Manufacturing LLC data center . The plan, which Imperial County officials voted to clear the way for in April, calls for a nearly 1-million-square-foot data center on parcels of unincorporated land just outside of Imperial, a city of about 22,000 people less than 15 miles from the U.S-Mexico border. Diana Salcedo at her home in Imperial. Salcedo is now part of a diverse new coalition of residents in California’s southeasternmost county that is harnessing anger over data centers into organizing around the November election in hopes of creating lasting change. She and others across Imperial County have begun writing letters and emails to politicians and showing up at meetings, sometimes for the first time in their lives. Some are running for local office themselves. The data center “activated a lot of us”, said Victor Zazueta, a retired librarian who on a September evening attended a letter-writing gathering in nearby El Centro. It was organized by Imperial Valley Get Organized! , or IVGO!, a new community group that is campaigning against incumbents on the county Board of Supervisors who supported the data center and supporting candidates for local elected office who prioritize the well-being of residents. The group of about 20 people gathered in a large meeting room at the back of the El Centro Police Activities League recreation center and included college students, retirees and residents from El Centro to Bombay Beach. The group formed only a few months ago and has encouraged candidates to run for El Centro City Council, the Imperial Valley Healthcare District and Seeley Union School District Board of Trustees in November’s election. From left: Fernando Marquez Duarte, Jake Tison and Jose Maldonado Mendoza gather with other residents for a letter writing event in September organized by Imperial Valley Get Organized! in El Centro. Salcedo, for her part, said she will not support Imperial County Board of Supervisors incumbents John Hawk or Jesus Eduardo Escobar, who both voted in favor of merging land parcels to allow the data center to move forward. Hawk, who did not respond to an emailed request for comment, is running against Patricia Lizarraga, and Escobar is running against Enrique “Kiki” Alvarado in November’s election. Both Lizarraga and Alvarado have said they will only consider supporting future data centers that have gone through environmental reviews. Escobar now says that his vote was a mistake. He said in an interview that he recognizes how upset constituents are about the data center project, with public outrage at county meetings at a level he had not seen since the COVID-19 pandemic. “It’s somewhat of a different flavor, because before it was blue against red for the most part. Not 100%, but for the most part,” Escobar said. “And now it seems that they’re united.” The groundswell of community organizing in Imperial County mirrors the opposition that has sprouted in communities across the United States, bringing people together across political party lines and other divisions against AI data centers in a way that few other issues have. Data centers have become a clear target for community organizing across the country because “people can actually see, like, ‘Oh, I’m upset about this thing, and there’s a very clear concrete thing to do about it, which is to try to get this blocked, to try to get this shut down,’” said Ben Green, an assistant professor of information and public policy at the University of Michigan. Many of the projects are being proposed for or built in rural areas, where there may be more land and infrastructure, but where there are also smaller communities in which people tend to know each other and government officials aren’t just anonymous figures, Green said. There is a sense among such residents that local governments are there to protect citizens and that they generally care about residents’ well-being, he said. That changed with data centers. “‘Who’s going to protect us if we don’t just get up and do it ourselves?’ is what people are now asking themselves,” Green said. “I think that’s what drives a lot of the organizing.” A campaign sign for Imperial County Supervisor John Hawk. There is also a political reality in a county of only about 180,000 people where elections can be won or lost by just a few hundred votes and small numbers of people can actually make a difference, whether it’s at public meetings or the ballot box. “It isn’t that hard to change the local government, which would be impossible to do in Los Angeles or San Diego without having a lot of money to inform a lot of people,” said Andra Dakota, a resident of Slab City near the eastern shore of the Salton Sea, who showed up to an IVGO! meeting last month. The current county supervisors should be very worried about the upcoming elections, she said, because they aren’t representing people’s interests: access to clean air and water, affordable homes, and a healthy environment in which to raise families. “We don’t want to be sold off to data centers and corporations,” she said. “We are interested in our people.” Salcedo started speaking out against the data center late last year at Imperial County Board of Supervisors meetings, something she had never done before in her decades living in the county. “You guys have to remember these are our homes!” Salcedo told supervisors at a January meeting while pounding her chest. “You are taking this away from us.” When it comes to Trump’s support for data center development in communities like hers, she said later, “He screwed up on this one.” Now, she said, when she gets mailers from Republican politicians asking her for donations, she sends them back not with money but with a note saying, “I’m not giving you guys a penny until you guys resolve this issue with the AI data centers.” The Imperial County Board of Supervisors has received the brunt of the backlash over data centers since it allowed the project to move forward. For months, heated public comment has dominated board meetings. At a March meeting, resident chants drowned out a presentation by Sebastian Rucci, the developer behind the proposed data center in Imperial. He ultimately left the meeting, and an angry crowd followed him to his car. Rucci’s company, Imperial Valley Computer Manufacturing, did not respond to a request for comment. Outraged residents have demanded an environmental review of the project, which would be built near homes and schools and have a large energy footprint. They questioned how the data center’s energy needs would be met when the local power grid already struggles on hot summer days. As the climate has warmed due to climate change, Imperial County’s infamous summer heat has become longer and more severe, leading to more frequent requests for residents to conserve energy. The Victoria Ranch housing community in Imperial is located next to the proposed site of a data center. When Imperial resident Christopher Scurries learned of the proposed data center, his first thoughts were about how it might affect his family. He worried that the family’s home value could plummet and that the quiet of his residential neighborhood in the Victoria Ranch development would be filled with an industrial hum. “I admit I felt maybe a little bit selfish at first,” he said. He grew concerned about the environmental effects of data centers and the ethical uses of artificial intelligence and started the group Not in My Backyard, Imperial that aims to educate the community about the data center proposal through social media posts. Until large data centers can operate ethically, Scurries said, he won’t support them in any communities. Related: Lithium Valley Dreams Meet Reality at Only Restaurant in California Town As in other parts of the country, many government officials in Imperial County initially viewed data centers as an opportunity for economic growth and a source of tax revenue. County officials heard the optimistic predictions about other industries and Imperial County became one of the leading producers of renewable energy in the state as a result. But jobs that were promised did not materialize on a large scale, and the county’s unemployment rate remains one of the highest in the state. Residents have voiced increasing skepticism about new industries such as lithium extraction and data centers, which were held up as future economic boons for Imperial County. Community members opposed to data centers hold signs at a Calexico City Council meeting in September during which council members voted to enact a ban on the facilities. Gilberto Manzanarez, an activist and former Calexico City Council member who works with Scurries’ NIMBY, Imperial, and other grassroots organizations, said he sees data centers as another extractive industry, just like solar and lithium projects that were also promised as a boon for the economically challenged region. “We’re just honestly so tired of it,” he said. Local organizing against data centers is having effects nationwide. From Georgia to California, local officials have heard calls from residents to place moratoria or bans on data center construction. In April, Imperial County supervisors approved a plan merging several lots of land owned by the data center developer. It was the only vote needed to allow the plan to move forward. After public backlash, they reversed course, enacting a 45-day moratorium on data centers in June. Although that moratorium was overturned in court, the county board again approved a moratorium at the beginning of October. The project has been stalled since Imperial County Superior Court Judge L. Brooks Anderholt, in a separate ruling in August, found county officials had illegally allowed the project to move forward without a state environmental review. Two supervisors, Escobar and Martha Cardenas-Singh, are pushing for a special election to allow residents to vote on the option to ban data centers on unincorporated land in Imperial County. Escobar said empowering voters to decide on the future of data centers is a way to offer transparency and accountability at a time when many residents are questioning the actions of the Board of Supervisors. Cardenas-Singh did not respond to an email requesting comment. Opponents of data centers gather and celebrate outside Calexico City Council chambers following a council vote that banned data centers in the city. Meanwhile, the movement against data centers has spread throughout Imperial County. At a September meeting, dozens of people, including a local real estate agent, educators, health care professionals and local activists, filed into the City Council chambers in Calexico to urge the border city of more than 38,000 to enact a data center ban. Many focused on the high rates of asthma and other respiratory illnesses in the community and the lack of benefits they see coming from a data center. “We are in a city where we are breathing in traffic air, breathing in pollution,” local teacher Roxsanna Pacheco said. “I’m trying to stay healthy. All of our community is trying to stay healthy. We do not need a data center.” The council approved the ban unanimously. On a state level, a slate of new laws will also make it harder for data centers to be built in California. Gov. Gavin Newsom signed several bills in September that will further regulate the industry in part by requiring disclosures of any environmental effects and mandating that new projects pay for their own electrical infrastructure. With the Imperial County data center project stalled, groups such as IVGO! are focusing their organizing on other local issues. At the group’s September meeting, Malik Glasgow sat at a round table with a few of his coworkers at a local nonprofit that supports individuals with disabilities and their families. With the encouragement of IVGO!, Glasgow, 33, is running for the Seeley Union School District Board of Trustees in November. Miroslava Cline, Sarah Khan Garcia, Marcie Landeros and Adriana Parga are also running for two seats in the at-large election. Malik Glasgow, left, and Jocelyne Garcia write letters to State Senator Steve Padilla at a letter writing event in El Centro. Glasgow became involved in community activism through his interest in environmental health in a county that struggles with air pollution from the U.S.-Mexico border and the shrinking Salton Sea and where nearly one in four elementary school children were diagnosed with asthma. As Glasgow learned more about local health disparities, he also learned about disinvestment locally. Glasgow said he is concerned about the effects of proposed lithium extraction projects and data centers and doesn’t think economic investment should come at the cost of public health or the environment. Instead, he sees education as a path to economic growth, and wants to start in his hometown. “I think that I can do enough to make change there,” Glasgow said. “Impactful change.” For Salcedo and other residents incensed over the data center proposal, the feeling of being betrayed by their elected officials can be deeply personal, they said. That’s especially true in a county as small as Imperial, where everyone seems to know each other and many community members have direct, personal relationships with their local government representatives, sometimes going back decades: They may have gone to high school together or attended the same church. Salcedo, for example, knew Peggy Price years before she chaired the county Board of Supervisors when they both worked for the county. When Price asked Salcedo if she could put campaign signs in front of her house for her supervisor’s race in 2024, Salcedo said yes. She voted for Price, and so did many of her neighbors. Price did not respond to an email requesting comment. So when Salcedo found out that Price had supported the data center proposal, it was “a slap in the face,” she said: She felt personally betrayed. Gina Brister Snow, left, and Steven Solis gather signatures to recall Imperial County Board of Supervisors Chairwoman Peggy Price. Now Salcedo is working on an effort to recall Price. That recall petition was approved by the county in October, and organizers are now collecting signatures to get it on a future ballot. Salcedo said she will keep going to government meetings, regardless of what happens with the data center proposed near her home. “I’m going to be paying attention now,” she said, “because I don’t trust them.”

articles.title: They Voted for Trump
articles.author: Gabriel Thompson
articles.content: The opinions expressed here are solely the author's and do not reflect the opinions or beliefs of the LA Progressive. On a sunny September afternoon, Juan Carlos stands behind the counter of his compact variety shop in California’s Central Valley, notes the lack of customers and pulls out a binder full of questions. During breaks, the slender 47-year-old is studying for his U.S. citizenship test. With business down 30% from a year ago, there’s plenty of time to study. “The other stores are also struggling,” he said. “Prices keep going up, so people are not spending.” Juan Carlos’ store, which sells a bit of everything — cowboy boots and piñatas, toiletries and backpacks — is in downtown Livingston, a small city in Merced County best known for its sprawling Foster Farms poultry plant and sizable Punjabi Sikh community. After living a more urban life in places including Oakland, Juan Carlos appreciates the slower pace of this city of 14,000, where the biggest event is an annual sweet potato festival. In interviews, locals tend to describe Livingston with words like quiet , diverse , safe . It is also politically unique: Livingston was the California city that swung most heavily for Trump , shifting 36 percentage points in his favor between 2020 and 2024. Other nearby cities tacked right as well. The November midterms promise to test the durability of that shift, especially among Latinos, a group Donald Trump made significant gains with in 2024. Voters in California’s Central Valley will help determine whether and how decisively Democrats retake the House of Representatives and gain new leverage to thwart the president’s agenda. Livingston, which is about 71% Latino , lies in California’s 13th Congressional District , which has a history of extraordinarily close races. In 2022, the moderate Democrat Adam Gray lost his campaign there by 564 votes; in 2024, he won by just 187 votes . His new Republican challenger, Kevin Lincoln, is a Trump-backed Marine veteran and former mayor of Stockton. Both candidates have campaigned on bringing down prices and making life more affordable. But interviews with Livingston residents underscore the stiff headwinds Lincoln faces. Take Juan Carlos. (At his request, Capital & Main is withholding his last name to protect his identity, as his U.S. citizenship application is still in process.) The shopkeeper said plenty of his Latino customers, who mostly work in the surrounding fields or the poultry plant, backed Trump in 2024. A Mexican immigrant, Juan Carlos understood the attraction: Though he couldn’t vote, he also supported Trump; his three adult children, who are U.S. citizens, all voted for him. Related: Fake ICE Officials Defrauding U.S. Families of Asylum Seekers “He has some racist ideas, but the economy will be better, the gas will be cheaper,” is how he described his thinking in 2024. Today, though, with gas in Livingston starting at around $6 a gallon and business slow, Juan Carlos and his kids have lost faith in Trump. “I thought it would all get better — but nothing is better,” he said. He is also newly anxious, which explains the binder full of citizenship questions. During a recent trip to Mexico, Juan Carlos was detained at the border, questioned extensively and released only after reaching his attorney. Although he has been a legal resident for more than a decade and owns his home and business, he felt the ground shift beneath him for a few frightening hours. The scare convinced him that he should forgo further trips abroad until he becomes a citizen. Gurpal Samra, a Livingston city councilmember whose family became the first of the Punjabi diaspora to move to the city in 1970, has seen a similar change in his community. Punjabis are an important voting bloc in Livingston, making up about 22% of the city. “We’re in the valley; it’s fairly conservative around here,” Samra said. “In the Indian community, we have a lot of farmers and truck drivers. They all went to support Trump because he said gas was going to be $2 a gallon. Now they’re not so happy.” Gurpal Samra is a member of the Livingston City Council and former mayor. Photo: Gabriel Thompson for Capital & Main. A Lot of Anxiety The 13th Congressional District encompasses all of Merced County, an agricultural area of about 300,000 residents, along with portions of neighboring counties. Last year, when voters approved Gov. Gavin Newsom’s redistricting in response to the Trump-backed remapping of Texas, the 13th was redrawn to include sections of Democratic-leaning Stockton. Gray, the district’s representative, is a Merced native who spent a decade in the California Assembly, where he founded the bipartisan Problem Solvers Caucus and focused on rural issues such as farming and water policy (as well as expanding health care access). Lincoln, his opponent, served as the mayor of the district’s largest city, Stockton, from 2021 to 2025, leaving the job after unsuccessfully challenging Rep. Josh Harder in California’s 9th Congressional District. Lincoln has criticized Gray for voting against Trump’s “One Big Beautiful Bill,” which cut social services to pay for tax cuts and an immigration crackdown, while highlighting his own Latino roots. (Lincoln’s mother is of Mexican descent; his father is African American.) Despite the election’s high stakes nationally, many local residents and business owners interviewed for this story weren’t particularly aware of it. Most of the political signs on display across the city are for candidates for City Council and school board. Yet federal policies over the last two years have certainly left their mark. “The kids have dealt with a lot of anxiety,” said Mario Alcazar, who was born and raised in Livingston and works as a high school counselor in the nearby town of Atwater. During heightened Immigration and Customs Enforcement activity in the area, he said, school attendance dropped for several days. “I would talk with a couple of my students who are undocumented about the classes they were going to take next year. One said, ‘Why are we talking about this when I might not be here?’ Their anxiety affects everything — their health, academics, relationships with friends.” Livingston resident Mario Alcazar stands in his front yard. Photo: Gabriel Thompson for Capital & Main. Federal immigration policies also fell heavily on the Sikh community, whose men disproportionately work in the trucking industry; by one estimate, they comprise 35% of the state’s commercial driver workforce. In September, the Trump administration issued new regulations targeting immigrant truckers that could lead to the cancellation of 61,000 truckers’ licenses , CalMatters reported. The state Department of Motor Vehicles already rescinded about 17,000 such licenses after a federal audit. “My uncle employed at least one or two young people who had their licenses canceled,” Livingston Councilmember Japjeet Singh Uppal said during a driving tour of the city. He passed by a vacant Rite Aid, the city’s lone bank and a Masonic lodge that is being converted into housing for veterans. Beyond downtown, the city has several parks and two domed Sikh temples, or gurdwaras, along with a handful of churches. “I went to one house where I met these four young guys who all lost their licenses,” said Uppal. “Now they’re doing DoorDash, Uber, whatever they can find. It’s had a huge impact, especially on younger men.” The administration intensified its targeting of Sikh drivers last month: A Homeland Security Department social media post depicted a Sikh man with the text “Get off our roads, you don’t know how to drive Mr. Singh,” “Self-deport or find out,” and “America for Americans.” The agency, which took down the post , said it was referring to Harjinder Singh, an Indian immigrant truck driver who has pleaded not guilty to criminal charges in a fatal crash in Florida. Singh, however, is a very common surname among Sikhs. Uppal, whose father was a trucker, said the Sikh community was “all in” for Trump in 2024 based on memories of the economy during his first administration. That’s changed dramatically. “I would hear this all the time from my own uncles: Business was booming, gas was cheap, truckers were getting solid rates on their loads,” he said. “Now they have their federal government calling all of them — or at least the truckers, which are a very prominent portion of the community — bad drivers that are at risk of deportation. It’s definitely been a 180 for a lot of people.” Massive Class Problem Although heightened immigration enforcement is a significant concern in Livingston, where about 40% of the population is foreign-born, the overriding issues there, as in the rest of the country, are high prices and the financial stress they cause. Not everyone, however, blames Trump. Brandon Friesen, whose family has run the town’s True Value hardware store for more than 60 years, considers California’s high gas taxes, decreased local oil production and government regulation the most significant obstacles to bringing prices down. “What California does has more effect on us than what Trump does, and California policies are more harmful,” he said. “We’ve changed light bulb sets about four times in the last 10 years to keep up with regulations. That ends up costing local people more money.” While Friesen appreciates that Gray “fights for local stuff,” he said he is also frustrated by the Democratic Party’s dominance in California and “looking for anyone that could disrupt the status quo.” Merced County Republican Chairman Gene Johnson echoed Friesen’s complaints about California regulations, but he also noted growing unease among local conservatives. During Trump’s first term and early in the current administration, he said, “Everyone was happy.” But now, he added, “All prices are up because of the Iran war. Most of the Republicans think the war should have been over by now.” Johnson, whose father was born in El Salvador, worries that Trump’s Latino backing in particular is eroding. “Trump got a lot of support from Latinos, but I think he’s lost quite a few of the ones that he gained,” he said. “People are paying $2,000 for a one-bedroom apartment. That’s very difficult, especially for Latinos in this area.” Mike Madrid, a political strategist who broke with the Republican Party after Trump’s first nomination, has been following voter sentiment in the Central Valley and predicts Gray will win easily. He sees the Latino shift away from Trump as having less to do with ethnic identity than the community’s working-class orientation. “Latinos have always been concerned … more about the economy and the cost of living than immigration issues,” Madrid said. “They can’t get ahead. They represent the massive class problem we have in America.” There are plenty of signs that residents of the 13 th District are struggling to meet their basic needs. “A year ago, we were distributing 1,000 pounds of food a week in Merced County,” said Terika Smith, who runs the local charity Food Para Todos. In one recent week, though, the group handed out 17,000 pounds. “We’ve never seen an increase this large. We have to turn people away at every distribution site.” Although Trump’s “Big Beautiful Bill” reduced funding for the Supplemental Nutritional Assistance Program by about $186 billion over 10 years and tightened work requirements, Merced County received a yearlong exemption due to high unemployment. Its number of SNAP recipients has remained steady as a result, according to Merced County’s Human Services Agency director, John Ceccoli. Hats Off While there haven’t been any public polls of the 13 th District in this cycle, the influential Cook Political Report moved the district from “toss up” to “lean Democratic” in January. And locals have their own way of tracking the political winds. “In the Punjabi community, it’s just been really quiet,” said Uppal, the councilmember. “Before, they were loud. Now they just don’t talk about politics anymore.” Livingston resident Elsa Rodriguez Juarez. Photo: Gabriel Thompson for Capital & Main. Elsa Rodriguez Juarez, a teacher in Livingston, said that while she could never support Trump due to his immigration policies, he initially represented “a sense of hope for some people” who were struggling economically. “You would often go to the grocery store in Livingston and see people wearing their Trump hats,” she said. Now, however, the president’s vocal local supporters have lowered their voices, Juarez said, “and I can’t tell you the last time I’ve seen somebody wearing that hat. Capital & Main

articles.title: Medicaid Cuts Pose Political Risk for Six-Term Congressman
articles.author: Elizabeth Aguilera
articles.content: The opinions expressed here are solely the author's and do not reflect the opinions or beliefs of the LA Progressive. Danielle Velling depends on monthly injections to keep her severe asthma at bay in California’s Central Valley, one of the most polluted regions in the U.S., where asthma rates exceed those in other parts of the state. She receives the medication thanks to Medicaid, the government-funded insurance program, known in California as Medi-Cal. But now she worries she could lose that insurance. Concern about cuts to health care prompted Velling, and dozens of others, to spend a record hot evening last month campaigning for upstart Democrat Randy Villegas. The college professor and local school board member aims to unseat longtime Republican Rep. David Valadao in a congressional race where access to health care has become a central issue. For Velling, it’s the difference between the freedom to live fully and having to constantly worry about whether she’ll be able to catch her breath. “One thing that shouldn’t be up and down is your health,” said Velling, 33. Related: Without Medicaid, How Many Rural Americans Will Die? Velling’s concerns highlight the political challenge facing Valadao, a six-term congressman whose district has one of the highest rates of federal Medicaid enrollment in the nation at 62%. Valadao voted for a bill that cuts the health insurance program for low-income people after promising that he would not support such an initiative. Valadao has said the program will continue to serve those who need it most. But an analysis of federal data by the Center for American Progress, a liberal think tank, estimates that more than 60,000 people in the district could lose their coverage starting in January. Democrats, hoping to capitalize on the changes brought by Proposition 50, the state ballot initiative which rewrote district lines to favor Democrats, have focused on health care and affordability, both pain points for voters in this election cycle. The race offers a rare opening in the majority Latino Central Valley, where the incumbent has repeatedly prevailed over his Democratic rivals, including in 2024 when he won 53.4% of the vote . The heavily agricultural 22nd Congressional District has a long history of conservative voting. It includes Bakersfield, part of Hanford, Porterville, Delano and Wasco, where about half a million people are enrolled in Medi-Cal, according to the Kaiser Family Foundation . Many more have friends or family who rely on the program. For Villegas, the fight over Medi-Cal is personal. “I am somebody who actually grew up relying on Medi-Cal and somebody who’s going to fight to restore that funding,” Villegas said the night the Bakersfield campaign office opened. It’s a line he repeats in many of his speeches and at rallies. “Nobody should have to choose between rationing their medicine and going to the doctor and paying for groceries,” he added. The son of Mexican immigrants, Villegas grew up working weekends at a swap meet and later in his family’s auto repair shop. He became the first in his family to go to college, eventually earning a doctorate degree and becoming a political science professor at College of the Sequoias in Visalia. He says programs such as Medi-Cal and the U.S. Special Supplemental Nutrition Program for Women, Infants and Children (known as WIC) helped make that path possible. Support for Villegas from volunteers and donors is fueled by their desire to unseat Valadao, whom they accuse of going back on his word. In February of 2025, incumbent Valadao said publicly that he would not support a bill that included reductions in Medicaid coverage. Five months later he cast the deciding vote for HR 1, the One Big Beautiful Bill Act. That legislation included changes to Medicaid that could eventually result in millions of people losing their insurance nationwide. Valadao’s campaign office did not respond to calls or emails for this story. But, in a televised debate between the candidates earlier this month, Valadao defended his vote for President Donald Trump’s signature legislation, arguing that the law will not deny health insurance to anyone the program is intended to help. “Medicaid was created to protect the most vulnerable, our elderly, our children and people with disabilities,” he said. “This [law] does not in any way shape or form affect anyone it was that the program was originally created for.” “It requires that people who have the ability to work that they actually show up and they try to work,” he added, referring to the new work requirements that are part of the law. “It’s not an actual cut.” The Congressional Budget Office estimates that 7.8 million people nationwide would lose insurance coverage by 2034 because of the new Medicaid rules, which include the work requirements, decreased eligibility for legal immigrants and more onerous reporting requirements. Valadao’s backers applaud his support for a law, which they say will reduce wasteful spending on Medicaid and other social programs while also providing tax breaks for families that need them. “He’s focused on affordability,” said Matthew Casarez, executive director of the Tulare County Republican Party. “He voted for tax cuts for working families, no tax on tips, no tax on overtime and no tax on social security for seniors.” Those tax breaks will expire in 2028 unless they are extended by Congress. Overall, the tax relief favors more affluent households, while the lowest-income households lose the most once cuts to Medicaid and food assistance are factored in , according to a report from the Congressional Budget Office. Casarez also touts Valadao’s strong ties to the residents in the district, and said his background as the son of immigrants and as a farmer are important to those who live in the Central Valley. In California’s salad bowl, the race has attracted national attention since California voters approved Proposition 50, allowing the state to redraw congressional districts to favor Democrats. The 22nd District was one of five targeted statewide, and The Cook Political Report rates the contest as a “toss up.” Villegas has aligned himself with the progressive wing of the Democratic Party led by Sen. Bernie Sanders of Vermont and New York’s Rep. Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez, who have both endorsed the Democratic candidate. Sanders, an independent who caucuses with the Democrats, showed up in Bakersfield on Oct. 4 for a “Fight Oligarchy” tour rally, walking on stage to greet Villegas to the “Power to the People” song. In late September, House Speaker Mike Johnson traveled to California to campaign for Valadao and other Republicans facing challenges in the aftermath of the Proposition 50 redistricting. It’s too soon to tell if a Villegas win will signal a move to the left on the part of voters — or if it’s a reflection of the anti-establishment mood that has beset voters. Political analyst Mike Madrid sees the race as part of a broader shift in which voters’ economic concerns are overriding traditional party loyalties. He expects Democrats to win key races like this one, where Valadao is facing voters stressed about making ends meet. “No amount of money can buy you out of bad fundamentals,” said Madrid, a founder of the Lincoln Project, a Republican anti-Trump political organization and an expert on Latino voters. “People know what they pay at the pump, they know what their health care premiums are, they know what their rent is going up to, they know unemployment is going up,” he added. Nevertheless, Villegas’ populist message — the Democratic candidate touts his support for Medicare for All and refuses corporate donations — may be helping to draw volunteers from across the district and the state. And his campaign has also drawn ardent support from those who have connections to the Medi-Cal program. In a district where nearly two-thirds of all residents and 87% of children rely on the program, many voters have used the program themselves, rely on it now or know someone who does. That includes Andrea Aldaz, 29, who came to Villegas’ Bakersfield campaign office to volunteer last month and continues to knock on doors for the candidate. She grew up on Medi-Cal just like many in her extended family. She now works for the Kern County Department of Human Services, where the majority of her clients are on Medi-Cal. Her mother is still on Medi-Cal and receives coverage for her diabetes through the program, Aldaz said. Medi-Cal pays for medication and transportation when her mom needs it. “It’s life,” Aldaz said. Audrey Chavez, a lifelong Bakersfield resident who runs Martin’s Meats & Deli with her husband, said she actively opposed the “Big Beautiful Bill.” Before the vote last year, she called Valadao’s office to urge him not to support it. “We can’t have that,” said Chavez, 59. “We have to have someone who’s willing to know our district, who knows the needs of the population and who speaks to those needs regardless of party.” Chavez, who along with her husband served hot taco plates from behind the food table at the Villegas event, used Medi-Cal during her four pregnancies, including one that ended in a miscarriage. Her concern now extends to customers and neighbors who depend on the program. “It doesn’t matter that it may not be me who is on Medi-Cal now,” Chavez said. “But it matters to me that it’s my customer who’s a senior citizen who relies on it or a veteran who relies on it or a young person that’s been unhoused that needs care.” This article was produced by Capital & Main .

articles.title: Trump's One-Man Horror Show Continues
articles.author: William J. Astore
articles.content: The opinions expressed here are solely the author's and do not reflect the opinions or beliefs of the LA Progressive. Donald Trump is a one-man horror show. Call him “annihilation man” for threatening to exterminate nearly 93 million Iranians for the crime of defying his will (and that of Israel and Netanyahu). I don’t write about Trump a lot because he’s so scrutable. He is what he is, an utterly shameless con man, a bullying narcissist who’s always on the make. What he isn’t, what he’s never been, what he never will be, is a public servant. Sadly, he has a lot of company. Few prominent politicians today really are, and if they are, the system does its best to corrupt them or expunge them if they can’t be corrupted. Trump came pre-corrupted, so to speak. Put more charitably, the powers that be determined they could live with Trump because he was so easily manipulated. Let him make some money, let him sign things with a Sharpie, let him pose and preen and insult, and otherwise flatter and cajole him in the direction you want him to go. Some Americans, Trump supporters of course, seem to think of Trump as a sort of lovable rogue. They laugh with, sometimes at, Trump while investing him with far more meaning than he has. It’s strange. They make apologies for him and think of him as being on their team. Related: Today's Tyrant Back in October 2016, I implored Americans to “dump chump Trump.” I remember getting a comment from a reader about my article, in which I contrasted my father’s character with that of Trump’s. Basically, the guy commenting said he preferred the kind of man Trump was. He really did emulate the bully, the braggart, the bigot in Trump. Perhaps because it gave him the excuse to be the same. Anyhow, here’s that article I wrote ten years ago this month . Obviously, America chose not to dump chump Trump, and so here we are, facing his many lamentable qualities, most especially his boasts about annihilating Iran just because they choose to resist his will. What kind of a presidential candidate tweets in the middle of the night about alleged sex tapes involving a former Miss Universe winner? Indeed, what kind of a man does this? Donald Trump is a chump. I’d call him a chimp, except it would be an insult to chimpanzees everywhere. The man has no discipline , no sense of decorum , and no compassion for others (let’s not forget his signature line, “You’re fired”). Indeed, he seems to revel in humiliating others. This was mildly amusing when he was taking on equals on the stage during the Republican primaries, but it’s disturbing in the extreme to see him bullying the little guys and gals for whom he’s supposedly a champion. So many sane people and major newspapers have gone on record as being against Trump that there’s little I can add. Sadly, Trump’s followers seem unperturbed and undisturbed no matter his insults and tyrannical behavior . All I can say is this: Trump is not the kind of man my father taught me to be. My dad, who fought forest fires in Oregon in the CCC, a veteran of an armored division in World War II, a city firefighter for more than 30 years until his retirement, treated people fairly and squarely. He was humble about himself and considerate to others. I can’t recall him insulting others, certainly not in the intentional and hurtful way that Trump directs at others. Trump is especially fond of attacking women or minorities or anyone he sees as vulnerable, the very opposite of my dad’s code of behavior. Don’t get me wrong: my dad wasn’t perfect. He had his faults. But his faults were not directed at others; he didn’t try to demean or diminish other people, as Trump so obviously enjoys doing. Unlike Trump, my dad wasn’t boastful; indeed, three favorite sayings of his were: “Still waters run deep,” “Don’t toot your own horn,” and “The empty barrel makes the most noise. ”You were right, Dad. The rushing nonsense from Trump exhibits his shallowness; the man is constantly tooting (or tweeting) his own horn; and, like the empty vessel that he is, he makes an awful amount of noise. Trump: Not the kind of man my father would respect; not the kind of man our country needs. Dump chump Trump.

articles.title: Upsurges Bubble Around the Globe but Will it Evolve into Effective Change?
articles.author: Michael Albert
articles.content: The opinions expressed here are solely the author's and do not reflect the opinions or beliefs of the LA Progressive. Reports show activism of many minds, addressing many topics and reaching considerable scale erupting in many places. Education, housing, corruption, jobs, prices, immigration, regimentation, fascism, war, data centers, weather, electoral campaigns, and more. France, Spain, Belgium, Albania, Brazil, Serbia, India, Nepal, Bangladesh, and more. What to do? On the one hand, where you are, if it arrives, participate. If it hasn’t yet arrived, try to initiate it. So far, so obvious. But a larger, overarching possibility beckons. Spread the eruption. Enlarge each outbreak. Make it all last. Still obvious. But how? What can turn a temporary eruption that may or may not win some specific immediately focused local aims into a sustained wave of activism that grows, persists and finally wins not only various initially sought aims, but whole new societies in a revolutionized world? Isn’t that the strategic question we must now address? Related: Rethinking Working-Class Resistance: Flipping the Script Without persistence we win some gains, but not many. We go a ways, but not far. To achieve more we must expand our efforts from upsurge to persistence. From single issue to multi issue. From public policy to systemic structure. And from shocking on-lookers to rousing and welcoming them. Upsurge alone may win some gains but it will not reach the causal core of society’s problems or potentials. To upsurge is not bad. Upsurges spread activism. To address a pressing issue is not bad. To address pressing issues inspires involvement and grows commitment. To overturn horrible public policy is not bad. To overturn public policies alleviates pain and teaches tactics. All of that counters passivity and fuels momentary hope. But significant victory requires sustained participation. To overturn the causes of contemporary suffering and attain preferred positive alternatives requires contagious persistent commitment. But how can we exceed our moment’s justified passions? How can initial narrowness reach out broadly? How can narrow focus diversify greatly? How can limited commitment deepen humanely? How can we develop sufficient coherence to confront and overturn existing institutions? How can we seek and finally implement a just, liberatory, self-managed future? For French high school students to demand equitable education is excellent. When they and their teachers and wider circles of workers and unions demand books not bombs, and then affordability for all, it makes critical connections that take resistance another step forward. When Spaniards add to demanding affordable housing, demanding quality education, it also takes a step forward. And when masses of neighborhood resisters add to ending corruption their desires to attain participatory democracy, or when union resisters add to preserving jobs desires to establish self-managed workers councils, or when consumer resisters add to attaining affordability desires to conceive and ultimately implement participatory planning, or when citizen resisters add to blocking fascism desires to enlarge participation, or everyone adds to ending war desires to wage peace, or adds to stopping data centers desires to develop people centers, or adds to ending fossil fuels desires to establish environmental justice, or adds to electoral campaigning desires to reconstruct governance, all that takes essential steps forward. But beyond diversifying, what can sustain upsurge? How does to briefly seek single issue public policy gains become to persistently seek multi-issue systemic institutional gains? If we don’t explore how movement enrichment can come about, how will we sensibly bring it about? Strategy can’t usefully be an afterthought of the decision to leave school, leave work, or leave home to go wild in the streets. Strategy has to propose flexible agendas—what to demand, what to close down, what to assemble. It has to conceive agendas for us to continually refine, correct, and implement in light of lessons we cull from experience. Whatever attracts more support, more participants, we do that. Whatever doesn’t. We reject that. Okay, but what features must a sustained multi-issue movement have that a single or even multi-issue upsurge needs to attain? How can those who desire fundamental change contribute to attaining those needed features? Persistent movements have participants who become driven by more than provocative slogans and desires. By more than anger and energy. Persistent movements have members whose wants grow beyond their initial passions. The mood and even the psychology of persistent movements’ members alters from short-term immediate spontaneous demonstrations to long-term carefully pursued plans. Activists’ moods rise beyond living to earn or living to survive, to living to win. Moods becomes confident but also careful, militant but also welcoming. Movements become alert to their implications. Indeed, persistent movements continuously calculate consequences. They pursue what will enlarge their numbers, deepen their commitment, and enrich their aims. They combine outreach with lasting organizational structure. They reject actions, words, or deeds that repel constituencies they need to attract. They pursue what will abet winning and reject what will obstruct winning. Upsurges happen when something that typically differs each time it appears—sometimes it may be masses volunteering, other times it may be masses rioting—ignites angry pain many others feel into positive demands for real gains. When something in whatever shape it emerges turns resigned acceptance of horrid, grim conditions to reasoned hope that strategic actions can and will yield better conditions. But to become sustained, strategic, and revolutionary requires more than a surge. Upsurge is in the air, more here, less there, to be sure—but if you look, you can see it happening or ready to happen there and here too, and maybe even all over. Will upsurge grow into sustained, collective, strategic commitment that persists until it achieves fundamental change? Upsurge is exciting. Upsurge is even wonderful. But its final grade depends on its consequences. I am 79. I was lucky to have participated in an earlier upsurge called the Sixties. It was heroic. It was solidaritous. It was passionate. It even spanned years. It won a lot but not fundamental change. We were insufficiently visionary for that. We were insufficiently strategic for that. We tried, but in the end, we did not win that. Ours was of course not the first upsurge that fell short or got waylaid. And there were more, too, between then and now. We lose, we lose, we lose, but when we learn sufficiently, we will win. I have always abhorred apocalyptic politics. But the simple fact is, the time has come to learn, to organize, and to fight until we win another world that is possible. And here, where I live perhaps close your eyes, open your mind, and listen to Leonard Cohen: It’s coming to America first, the cradle of the best and of the worst. It’s here they got the range It’s here they got the range and the machinery for change and it’s here they got the spiritual thirst. It’s here the family’s broken and it’s here the lonely say that the heart has got to open in a fundamental way: Democracy is coming to the U.S.A. Or if you prefer, listen to young Bobby: Oh, the foes will rise With the sleep still in their eyes And they’ll jerk from their beds and think they’re dreamin’ But they’ll pinch themselves and squeal And know that it’s for real The hour when the ship comes in Then they’ll raise their hands Sayin’ we’ll meet all your demands But we’ll shout from the bow your days are numbered And like Pharaoh’s tribe They’ll be drownded in the tide And like Goliath, they’ll be conquered This article was produced by Z Network .

articles.title: World Record Presidency
articles.author: Steve Hochstadt
articles.content: The opinions expressed here are solely the author's and do not reflect the opinions or beliefs of the LA Progressive. Although the Nobel Prize for Peace has eluded Donald Trump thus far, proper recognition of his peacemaking abilities will certainly come eventually. In the meantime, I believe that his unprecedented achievements should be enumerated and recognized. I propose to seek the approval of that arbiter of the extraordinary, the Guinness World Records, for Trump’s supremacy in the following categories, only a sampling of the possibilities. Largest number of high-ranking female administration officials, personally chosen, fired in one week. See stories about Kimberly Ann Guilfoyle and Kate Sharon Zacharia. The tidbit that one announced the firing of the other cannot be encompassed in a category. Most dollars taken in by a President. Subcategories: in one month; in one year; in an entire term. Amounts already qualify; total to be calculated in 2029. Most dollars taken in by a President’s family. Related: Comeuppance This is a necessarily separate, but related category. Most lies told as official statements. Subcategories could be infinitely multiplied, so let’s settle for one total award. The Washington Post has done the work. Most leading Black women verbally attacked, lifetime award. See Lisa Cook, Letitia James, and Fani Willis. Evidence for this category does not include the disproportionate loss of jobs by Black women due to Trump’s policies. Most announcements that a war is over, while that war continues. Most demands that immediate subordinates verbally attest to his greatness, per month during a presidency. First demand in history that a rally audience makes the same claims. Most rejections of lawsuits at the federal level. Difficult to quantify, but clearly beyond any previous contestant. Most physical destruction of federal property in a term. Most physical destruction of the White House complex. Important to make this a separate category. Largest vote-buying proposal in world history. $5000 per American adult would total more than one trillion dollars. In consideration is a separate category for most vote-buying schemes at the state level . Most significant prevention of wind power production. Related: Two Sides of Trump’s Mouth There are no other contestants. Most extensive use of gold paint in the Oval Office. Most racist set of presidential policies. More research must be done to verify that Trump deserves this award against other contenders, such as Woodrow Wilson and Andrew Johnson. Most career expert appointees replaced by political supporters. I’m just guessing here about a category that would be difficult to quantify. The Great Replacement goes on: see reporting by Dan Diamond in NYT October 21. Some categories might not be appropriate for Guinness World Records, but the outstanding, even unique nature of Trump’s performance must be considered in any judgment about his world record presidency. “The most regressive tax and budget legislation in modern American history.” Quoted from a recent paper by Yale scholars Patrick Sullivan and Jacob S. Hacker, referring to the 2025 One Big Beautiful Bill Act. Most imperialist and aggressive policy against neighboring and allied lands in modern history. This could be phrased as “largest number of new US states proposed by conquest”. Nastiest presidential comments about federal judges. Of course, judgments about the nastiness level of particular epithets are idiosyncratic. However, adding together the following: "Wacky, Nasty, Crooked, and totally Out of Control Judge" about U.S. District Judge James Boasberg; “completely inept and embarrassing Court” and “fools and lapdogs” about Supreme Court justices, in particular, Neil Gorsuch and Amy Coney Barrett, who "sicken me"; “crazed lunatic” about U.S. District Judge Ana Reyes; and many others, creates an unbeatable record. Largest drop in the outside world’s approval of America in one term. Although this category is notoriously difficult to measure, its worldwide reach makes winning it a notable achievement. The drop in approval of the US across 20 countries from 54% in 2024 to 36% in 2026 demonstrates the global effects of Trump’s actions. Trump may not always be the best, but even second-place finishes add to his luster. Trump has the lowest approval rating at midterm since Harry Truman in 1946 . I hope that Trump’s well-known identity as a teetotaler will not prevent Guinness from recognizing his achievements. One final category, to be held in abeyance until after November 3: Caused greatest electoral wipeout in American history.

articles.title: A New Israeli Government Won’t Stop the Settlements
articles.author: Diana Buttu
articles.content: Next Tuesday, Israel will hold its first general election since the October 7 attacks and the destruction of Gaza. The election campaign has again illustrated the radicalization of Israeli politics, even beyond Benjamin Netanyahu’s government, and the breadth of political forces who staunchly resist the creation of a Palestinian state. In an interview, Palestinian Canadian lawyer and analyst Diana Buttu, who lives in Haifa, explains why she will cast her ballot in this election while rejecting Israel’s claim to be a democracy. Speaking to Elias Feroz for Jacobin , she discusses what a change of government could — and could not — mean for Palestinians, the new death penalty law, and the planned Palestinian elections next month. Elias Feroz Recent polls indicate that Benjamin Netanyahu may be on course to lose power. However, his government’s policies toward Palestinians have been supported by a much broader political establishment. If Netanyahu loses the election, what would actually change for Palestinians? Diana Buttu I think there are several ways of looking at politics inside Israel. In some ways, one can say that it’s all the same, and, in part, it is. But we also need to look at who is going to be around Netanyahu and who is going to be prime minister. Over the past three years, people like Bezalel Smotrich and Itamar Ben-Gvir have pushed some of the worst policies toward Palestinians. I’m not under any illusion that a new prime minister would stop the settlements. But I do think that the extreme harm and this path of evil they have created could change, even if only slightly. In particular, I’m looking at people like Itamar Ben-Gvir, who has normalized torture, the arming of Israelis, and the killing of Palestinians. Recently, he posted this concentration-camp-like video on his social media account [the video has since been deleted from Ben-Gvir’s account on X]. People like Ben-Gvir, Smotrich, Netanyahu, and Heritage Minister Amichai Eliyahu, who said Israel “must find ways for Gazans that are more painful than death,” are fascists. They must go. We have to do what is necessary to prevent them from continuing to have the immunity to carry out these crimes. Elias Feroz Do you intend to vote in the upcoming elections in Israel? Diana Buttu Yes, I do. I can only speak for myself, but I know that Israelis are always going to find someone to represent me. So why not choose my own representative? That doesn’t mean I believe in the Israeli system or in Israeli democracy. I don’t. The system is racist and designed to try to get Palestinians out. But if I have the opportunity to vote, I will. I want to be represented. Our struggle as Palestinians living here is to survive and remain on our land. We are the survivors and descendants of those who survived the Nakba. When you see that 75 percent of the population was ethnically cleansed, and that so many more remain under Israeli military rule, you understand that our struggle is simply to remain in our country and on our land. Elias Feroz What does political representation mean to you personally? Diana Buttu I was born and raised in Canada because my parents left Palestine. They left because they could no longer cope with living under a racist system. Other members of my family also left, looking for a better education and a better life. Many of them never came back. That is exactly what I don’t want to happen to the next generation. Today our students have more opportunities to study in Jordan, the West Bank, and elsewhere, in their own language, with degrees that are recognized. I want my children to be able to get an education in their own language and live in Palestine. That is what I believe our representatives should be doing: increasing our sumud [Arabic for “steadfastness”]: our ability to remain in our country, on our land, with our identity, rather than constantly thinking about leaving. I believe people will only stay when they have someone representing their interests. Elias Feroz You have Israeli citizenship and the right to vote, but you’ve said that you don’t believe in Israeli democracy. Why is that? Diana Buttu Because there are different classes of citizens within the country. Any Jewish person from anywhere in the world can immigrate to Israel. What does that tell you? It tells you that Israel is first and foremost a Jewish state. If it was truly a democracy, my aunt — who was born and raised in Palestine, married there, and had her first child there — should have had the same right to return as any Jewish person. But in 1948, she became a refugee. She could never return and eventually died in a refugee camp in Jordan. I’m a citizen. My father is a citizen. Why couldn’t she return then? That’s where the contradiction becomes clear. They try to reconcile Israel being both a democratic and a Jewish state, but they know that the two cannot have equal priority. At some point, one has to come first. Israelis usually say that there are democratic elements, but they recognize that the system itself is not democratic. The fact that I can vote doesn’t change that. It simply means I get to choose a representative. It doesn’t change the fact that the state privileges Jewish citizens over everyone else. My right to vote does not make me fully equal. If I were fully equal, I would be able to purchase land anywhere in the country. I wouldn’t be excluded from places because I’m considered undesirable or not part of the community. That’s what democracy would mean: full equality. Dropping a ballot into a ballot box doesn’t undo the racist apartheid nature of the state. Elias Feroz After nearly two decades without national legislative elections, Palestinians in the West Bank, Gaza, and East Jerusalem are due to vote for a new legislative council on November 28. What do you expect these elections to change in Palestinian politics? And how realistic are these elections, given Israel’s control over East Jerusalem and the devastation and displacement in Gaza? Diana Buttu First, I don’t know if the elections will actually happen. The last elections were in January 2006, and parliament stopped meeting in March 2007. Since then, President Abu Mazen [i.e., Mahmoud Abbas], who can hardly be called that at this point, has been ruling by presidential decree, even though his term expired a long time ago. If the elections happen, I hope that his ability to rule by decree will be challenged. Presidential rule without checks and balances is effectively a dictatorship. Elections could give new life to the idea of leadership and representation. And when I say new life to leadership, I mean a very limited framework. I’m only talking about the small percentage of land and the small percentage of people [that are under the administration of the Palestinian Authority (PA)]. I’m well aware that you can’t have real democracy under occupation. But at the same time, I think it’s also important for us to once again be able to choose our own leaders. Elias Feroz If Palestinians elect a new government, what power would it actually have? Israel continues to control large parts of the West Bank, while settlement expansion is accelerating. And with the planned construction in the E1 corridor, which would effectively cut through the West Bank and further isolate East Jerusalem, how much political authority would a Palestinian government be left with? Diana Buttu There are different levels that we’re talking about here. So first, again, it’s easy to say there’s nothing left. I’m well aware that the Palestinian Authority’s territory has always been very limited in size. But the issue today is also about representation. Abbas was elected in 2005 for four years. He’s been in office now for twenty-one years. If we have elections, he’s going to be ninety-one. I do think it’s important for us to be able to choose a next generation that isn’t in their nineties. So let’s look at the alternatives. What if we don’t have elections? Do we just wait for him to die? I think this election is going to be about the people and about what the future looks like. Is it going to be a future in which the Israelis choose our leaders for us? One in which Abu Mazen chooses who the next person is? Or is it going to be us who choose? I don’t think there’s anything the PA can do on the ground. We know they’re not going to be able to send an army to protect us from violent settlers. They don’t have the army or the territorial jurisdiction, and we know they would be gunned down. But isn’t it their duty to at least speak out, to try to get international attention and support, while the Israelis are carrying out an active campaign to get rid of the Palestinian Authority? Look at these past three years of genocide. Do I think that the Palestinian Authority has done a great job when it comes to this genocide? Absolutely not. I think their one job over the past three years has been to be the voice of the people who are going through genocide. The other thing, however, is that Israel also doesn’t want any elections to happen. They’re happy with Abu Mazen being in power because he does exactly what they want him to do. He doesn’t push back. He’s viewed as weak, and they can point to him and blame him whenever anything happens. Elias Feroz In the past, you have described the Palestinian Authority as a “security subcontractor” for Israel and argued that Oslo created a Palestinian government responsible for maintaining internal security but without sovereignty. Diana Buttu I wrote that in 2017 and it’s only gotten worse. One of the reasons I said the PA had to throw in the towel was because they weren’t doing what they were supposed to do, which is represent Palestinians. Instead, they were going down the path of thinking the only way to represent Palestinians was effectively giving in to whatever the Israelis told them to do. That hasn’t changed and that’s why I say it’s time for a change in leadership. Now, to be absolutely clear, one of the main problems is that Abu Mazen has now set up an electoral system in which he is effectively the one who chooses who can run and who can’t, because he has changed the electoral laws. There are going to be some political parties who will abide by that and go along with it for pragmatic reasons, because they view his removal as being very important. Elias Feroz If Palestinians elect a new legislative council in November, do you believe the Palestinian Authority can still be transformed into a genuine instrument of Palestinian self-government? Diana Buttu Yes, but it requires active participation and a lot of thinking. It requires creating a different way of thinking that goes beyond the Palestinian Authority. Until now, nothing has happened, in part because the PA has crushed every attempt to create something new. Elias Feroz Germany, France, the United Kingdom, Italy, the Netherlands, and Norway, together with Canada, have strongly condemned Israel’s decision to move ahead with the E1 settlement project, warning that it would drive a wedge through the West Bank and undermine the possibility of a viable Palestinian state. What do you make of this condemnation? Does that represent a meaningful shift in European policy toward Israel? Diana Buttu When I first moved to Palestine, almost twenty-six years ago, I started noticing a pattern of condemnation after condemnation. Back then in 2000, there were around four hundred thousand settlers in the West Bank. We’re now talking about close to eight hundred thousand settlers. You mean to tell me those condemnations did something? No, they did nothing. They could have stopped the number of settlers from doubling over those twenty-five years if they had taken action. It got to the point, around 2007, where I noticed they were effectively copying and pasting the same condemnations. If you look at a condemnation from 2010 and one from 2018 — they’re practically the same, almost word for word. Amid the genocide, around forty thousand settlement units have been in the planning process over the past two years, from 2023 to 2025. So all these countries condemning Israel doesn’t have any impact. Israel can handle the condemnations. What it can’t handle is action: cutting off trade relations, boycotting it, imposing sanctions, and not sending weapons. Elias Feroz Another subject that has sparked criticism is Israel’s new death penalty law. It primarily affects Palestinians in the occupied territories who, unlike you, do not possess Israeli citizenship and hence are subject to Israel’s military justice system, without having a vote or political representation in Israel. At the same time, Israeli settlers who kill or expel Palestinians in the West Bank are often protected by the military. Diana Buttu To be clear, under the military court system the death penalty has always been an option. It has been part of the military law since it came into effect in 1967. But very early on, Israel made a policy decision not to seek the death penalty. That has now changed. They have removed that policy and made the death penalty mandatory for people convicted of what they call “nationalistic crimes,” while at the same time they have significantly limited the appeals process. Elias Feroz What are “nationalistic crimes” according to the new law? Diana Buttu The law targets killings committed as part of what is defined as a “nationalistic” or “terrorist” crime, particularly where the perpetrator denies the existence of the State of Israel. Then there’s the other track, which is the civil law under the Israeli system. This system applies both to Israelis and Palestinians who have an Israeli citizenship. Hence, Israeli settlers are prosecuted under the civil system. Let’s take the example of Israeli settlers killing Palestinians. Even if these acts are considered acts of terror, they would not fall under this law because the settlers are not acting against the [Israeli] state. In fact, they are acting in its name. What the law is really targeting, then, are cases in which the person killed is Israeli. A Palestinian living in the West Bank who tries to resist settler attacks will be punished by death. The law is criminalizing resistance to occupation, which is a right enshrined in international law. I know there are lawyers who are going to challenge the law, and I wonder how successful those challenges will be. Elias Feroz Despite the so-called ceasefire, over a thousand more Palestinians have been killed and thousands injured; the seizure of UNRWA [United Nations Relief and Works Agency for Palestine Refugees in the Near East] facilities in East Jerusalem was celebrated by Ben-Gvir; Israel is threatening to expand its attacks in Gaza over kites and balloons in the sky; and an Israeli Knesset member even destroyed a Palestinian monument in the West Bank. As a lawyer, how do you explain this apparent disregard for international law? Diana Buttu The international legal system takes a very long time, and it’s reluctant to act unless it deems something to be a threat to peace and security. Even though it’s supposed to get involved and act to stop genocide, it doesn’t, because its wheels are too slow. And when it comes to Palestine, I’ve noticed that the world waits for a critical breaking point, and even then, they’re not willing to act. On top of that, we’re dealing with a crazy man in the White House, and the whole world seems to be caught up with him. All of this creates a recipe for continued genocide. The other thing is European guilt over the Holocaust. Don’t get me wrong, Europe should feel guilty about it. But this guilt shouldn’t come at the expense of the Palestinians. We have report after report: How many more reports do we need about genocide? How many more scholars? How many more UN accounts? How much more does Israel need to do before the world recognizes that this is genocide? Elias Feroz South Africa has now asked the International Court of Justice (ICJ) to address Israel’s noncompliance with its orders in the Gaza genocide case. What, in your view, can the court actually do if Israel continues to ignore its orders? Diana Buttu International law is very different from domestic law. Under domestic law, the law applies to everybody within a territory, whether you’re in Canada, Germany, or the United States. There’s a parliament that passes the laws, there are enforcement mechanisms, and you can be thrown in prison if you violate them. The international system works very differently. It’s about relations between states. There is no parliament and no general enforcement mechanism. The main enforcement mechanism that exists is when there is a threat to international peace and security. The closest thing to a parliament is the system of treaties, where countries sign on and give their consent. But the Genocide Convention is considered one of those treaties that applies to all countries. It’s not simply a matter of whether a country chooses to consent — all countries are bound by it. Israel, in any case, has also consented to the Genocide Convention. What does that mean? It means that countries around the world have an obligation to make sure that genocide does not occur. And they have various ways of doing that: they can cut off trade, boycott, impose sanctions, or even seek to exclude Israel from the UN. The most basic thing is to cut off arms supplies. However, countries are unwilling to go down that path, even though it’s very clear what Israel is doing. Instead, they’re waiting for a judicial determination. In other words, they’re waiting for the ICJ. The problem is that this final case is going to take years. And by then, it’s going to be too late. By then, the world will say, “All right, too bad. But it already happened. Let’s move on.” This article originally appeared in Jacobin , a democratic socialist magazine publishing long-form essays and analysis on politics, economics, and culture.
