articles.title: Food as an Act of Resistance
articles.content: The Thirty-Second Art Bulletin (October 2026) The images in this art bulletin are from the exhibition MST: 40 Years , an online exhibition of illustrations celebrating four decades of struggle for land and agrarian reform by Brazil’s Landless Rural Workers’ Movement (MST) , organised in partnership with Tricontinental: Institute for Social Research and other organisations. Listen to ‘ A desalambrar ’ (Tear Down the Fences!), written and performed by Uruguayan singer-songwriter Daniel Viglietti and also performed by Chilean singer-songwriter and theatre director Víctor Jara. ‘A desalambrar’ raises a fundamental question: who owns the land, and who has the right to cultivate it? The song’s call for agrarian reform and collective control over the resources that sustain life resonates with the struggle for food sovereignty. Every 16 October, on World Food Day, La Via Campesina and its member organisations around the world mobilise for the International Day of Action for Peoples’ Food Sovereignty and against Transnational Corporations. Their mobilisation affirms that food systems should serve peoples’ needs and protect nature rather than generate profits. The movement also calls for the defence of peasant seeds – seeds that farming communities have cultivated, selected, saved, and exchanged over generations – and communities’ rights to save, reproduce, exchange, and sell them. To explore how the struggle for food sovereignty extends from the land to the kitchen, encompassing the preservation of seeds, cultural knowledge, and collective traditions, we interviewed four cooks, chefs, and organisers. Anita Epulef Panguilef , a Mapuche cook and seed keeper from Curarrehue in Chile’s Araucanía Region, demonstrates how food sovereignty is practised through everyday relationships with land, water, biodiversity, and community. Norma Listman and Saqib Keval, chefs and co-owners of Masala y Maíz in Mexico City, explore the connections between Mexican, South Asian, and East African culinary traditions, using cooking to recover histories obscured by colonialism and shaped by migration and displacement. Ana Chã, a member of the MST and coordinator of the Elza Soares Cultural Centre in São Paulo, explains how these practices become part of a collective political project in which the struggle for land extends all the way to the table. Together, their experiences show that defending food sovereignty means defending more than what ends up on our plates. It means defending peoples’ right to decide what is planted, who grows it, which seeds circulate, how food is prepared, whose knowledge is recognised, and how communities gather to eat. Credit: Ricardo Keferaus. In Curarrehue, nestled among the mountains, forests, and rivers of southern Chile, Anita Epulef reminds us that food sovereignty is not an abstract concept but an everyday practice that begins long before a pot is placed over the fire. Her daily life involves selecting seeds for planting, preparing a trafkintu (a traditional Mapuche gathering for exchanging seeds and knowledge), checking whether frost has damaged the plants, gathering food from the vegetable garden, observing streams and other waterways, tending to lawen (medicinal plants), reading the clouds, and greeting fellow community members. She describes these practices as a dialogue with itrofillmogen , a Mapuche concept encompassing the diversity of life and the relationships among all living beings. The word ‘Mapuche’ itself means ‘people of the land’. The name expresses more than an identity tied to a particular territory. For Anita, the relationship with the land shapes people’s understanding of nourishment, health, knowledge, and responsibility. ‘If the land becomes sick, the food becomes sick too’, she explains. Caring for the land therefore means caring for life. Yet this relationship is threatened by the growing concentration of agricultural land in fewer and fewer hands. According to a 2026 report jointly published by the Food and Agriculture Organisation of the United Nations (FAO), the International Land Coalition, and the French Agricultural Research Centre for International Development, there are approximately 570 million farms worldwide. About 85% of the world’s farms are smaller than two hectares, yet they account for only 9% of agricultural land. By contrast, farms larger than 1,000 hectares represent just 0.1% of all farms but operate more than half of that land. The report also finds that the largest 10% of landholders operate 89% of the total. The struggle over food therefore begins with the struggle over the means of producing it: land. Credit: Marieli Ribeiro. This understanding is central to the MST’s struggle for food sovereignty in Brazil. Ana Chã explains that land provides the material basis for communities to decide what to produce, how to live, how to care for nature, and how to organise themselves. Access to land alone, however, is not enough if farmers remain dependent on corporate seeds, agrochemicals, other agricultural inputs, and markets controlled by large companies. Control over seeds is therefore also essential to food sovereignty. ‘Seeds are everything’, Anita tells us. In her community, saving seeds allows families to plant their own crops and produce food for the coming winter without depending on commercial seed suppliers. But this autonomy is threatened by efforts to privatise seeds that communities have freely saved and exchanged for generations. For Anita, such efforts threaten not only communities’ ability to produce food independently but also their collective knowledge and memory. She describes this as an act of ‘robbing the memory of a people’. The loss of seed diversity is another concern. FAO has long cited an estimate that around 75% of crop genetic diversity was lost during the twentieth century, as farmers increasingly replaced local varieties – including those adapted to local growing conditions over generations – with genetically uniform, high-yielding varieties. When a seed variety disappears, the possibility of cultivating it is lost, while the knowledge of how to grow, preserve, prepare, and pass it on to future generations is also put at risk. For La Via Campesina, the defence of peasant seeds is at the heart of the struggle for food sovereignty . The movement calls on peasant families and communities to become guardians of seeds, ensuring their preservation, reproduction, exchange, and collective protection. The struggle over seeds does not end in the fields. It continues in the kitchen, where food is prepared, shared, and remembered. Credit: Camila Camomila. For Anita, the connection between land, seeds, and food is also reflected in the ingredients she uses – gathered from local forests and vegetable gardens or grown from locally cultivated seeds. Her account brings together the autumn gathering of ngülliw (seeds from the pewen , or monkey puzzle tree), the harvesting of broad beans by older women in the community, the gathering of lleuques (fruit from the Chilean plum yew) by young people, and the smoking and cooking of chillies over a wood fire. Together, these practices reflect the relationship between food, land, and the transmission of knowledge across generations. Preserving agricultural diversity is also a way of ensuring that communities can continue to grow their own food. For Anita, keeping several varieties of potatoes, for example, is not merely a matter of taste. If a variety disappears from the market, the community can still grow it. When she teaches someone to grind chilli, she also tells them how her grandmother used it. In this way, knowledge passes ‘from hand to hand’. Traditional or ancestral knowledge is not a fixed collection of dishes from the past. It is practical knowledge accumulated over generations: knowing when to plant, which seeds are suited to a particular climate, which plants can be gathered from the forest, how food can be preserved, the medicinal properties of plants, how recipes change with the seasons, and how this knowledge is passed on. Norma Listman and Saqib Keval similarly challenge the idea that culinary traditions are confined within national borders. At their restaurant, Masala y Maíz, they draw on histories of migration and exchange connecting Mexico, South Asia, and East Africa. Their dishes combine native Mexican maize, wild quelites (edible wild greens), cacao, vanilla, and Mexican chillies with South Asian and East African ingredients and cooking techniques. For Norma and Saqib, sourcing native and traditional ingredients is ‘non-negotiable’. They argue that every peso spent on a native variety helps sustain its cultivation and keep its seeds in circulation, rather than contributing to its disappearance under industrial agriculture. But they also insist that chefs must look beyond the ingredients themselves and recognise the labour and knowledge of the people who cultivate them. Established chefs often have access to financial resources and public platforms that many agricultural producers lack. Norma and Saqib argue that this privilege comes with a responsibility to pay producers fairly and consistently, acknowledge their contributions publicly, and support the preservation of the agricultural knowledge behind each dish. Credit: Estela Carvalho. For Anita, cooking with young people, women, and children is an opportunity to share stories while preparing food together. As the water boils for soup, people chop, knead, talk, and remember. She teaches because she does not want younger generations to feel the same shame about their traditional foods that previous generations experienced. The kitchen becomes a place where language, memory, and cultural pride are passed on along with culinary knowledge. ‘When I teach, I am defending Mapudungun’, Anita explains, referring to the Mapuche language, which is preserved through the names of ingredients and traditional practices. Her everyday activities – from tending the garden to cooking for her family and visitors – become ways of defending her community’s relationship with the land. Norma and Saqib describe a similar process of preserving cultural knowledge through recipes. Recipes can survive displacement, migration, colonisation, famine, drought, and genocide because they can be passed down through generations and recreated in everyday life. They do not depend solely on written records or institutions for their survival. Instead, they are preserved and transformed as people cook, adapt, teach, and share them. Preserving culinary knowledge is therefore less about maintaining an unchanging tradition than ensuring its continuity across generations. Credit: Pablo Placencia Lagos. Ana Chã explains that collective kitchens are among the first spaces established in the MST’s encampments and also play an important role in the movement’s schools, cooperatives, meetings, and training centres. In these spaces, people share responsibilities, exchange knowledge and memories, build relationships, and prepare meals together. Through its Cozinhas Sem Terra (Landless Kitchens), the MST prepares healthy food using locally produced ingredients whenever possible while celebrating the culinary traditions of different regions of Brazil. A meal can connect the person who saves the seed to the person who grows the crop, the person who cooks it, and the person who eats it. In doing so, it can make visible the people and the labour behind food – connections often obscured by the industrial food system. For Ana, this collective approach to food is also a form of resistance to a system that treats food as a commodity and makes people increasingly dependent on large corporations. Recovering a grandmother’s recipe, planting a crop variety at risk of disappearing, exchanging seeds, bringing food from agrarian reform settlements to a school or urban community, organising a food fair, or teaching children where their food comes from are all ways of strengthening communities’ control over food and preserving the knowledge associated with its production and preparation. These practices are part of the MST’s broader vision of popular agrarian reform, which links the democratisation of access to land with agroecology, seed protection, biodiversity, healthy food, cooperation, fair markets, the recovery of food cultures, and alliances between rural and urban communities. This is food sovereignty as praxis: a political project realised through everyday collective action. Although rooted in different histories and experiences, Anita’s seed keeping, Norma and Saqib’s cooking, and Ana’s organising through the MST all raise a common question: who gets to decide how food is produced and how the knowledge associated with it is preserved and passed on? Credit: Madalena Ayam Ubrais Barco. Food sovereignty means returning control over how food is produced and shared to peoples and communities. But protecting seeds and securing land are only part of the struggle. As Ana reminds us, food sovereignty also requires transforming how we grow, prepare, eat, and share food, as well as our relationship with nature. On 16 October, movements around the world once again affirmed that food is not merely a commodity. The challenge is to make this conviction a reality – in the soil, through seeds, in the kitchen, and at the table. Anita offers a powerful metaphor for this struggle: ‘Every time I cook, for my family or in public, every interview, every post, every conversation is a trench.’ But a trench is not only a place to defend what remains. It is also a place to plant the seeds of a different future. Warmly, Soledad Varela Operations Manager, Tricontinental: Institute for Social Research Soledad studied culinary arts at the Escuela Culinaria Francesa in Santiago, Chile.

articles.title: Latin America: the ‘cultural battle’ as a facade for neoliberalism
articles.author: Pablo Meriguet
articles.content: For several years now, politicians, influencers, and intellectuals from Latin America’s new radical right have been speaking about the importance of the “cultural battle” to recover a sort of perspective lost in the past and to underpin a civilizational project that prioritizes the individual, individual freedom, and the free market above all else. Probably the first to insist on this idea in the media was Javier Milei, the current president of Argentina, who initially made a name for himself as an economist who had no problem insulting his opponents and defending orthodox neoliberal thought. At that time, Milei, along with his intellectual allies, called for a stand against a purported culture imposed by so-called left-wing elites who had tarnished common sense, Christian morality, and individual freedom, among many other things. A few days ago, Colombian President Abelardo de la Espriella called for a radicalization of his “cultural battle” and ordered the removal of dozens of works of art from various museums in order to restore a culture that has been held captive by the left, Marxism, and other dark (or, as Milei himself puts it, “demonic”) forces. In reality, the move isn’t particularly original. Back in the United States, Pat Buchanan (a close advisor to Nixon and Reagan) had already advocated for and encouraged inflammatory rhetoric to wage a “culture war” and thus defend a culture tarnished by social change. Among the major intellectual inspirers of this doctrine are the American Sam Francis and the Frenchmen Alain de Benoist and Guillaume Faye (albeit with their well-known differences). Even some Germans in the 1930s attempted to make what they called “cultural Bolshevism” the scapegoat for all their ills. But the push for a “cultural battle” in Latin America had a more interesting rationale. And it is not so much due to a supposed pragmatic interpretation of Antonio Gramsci’s concept of hegemony – which has been distorted by the new radical right, as well as by much of liberalism and social democracy, which understand it solely as “cultural hegemony.” No, in reality, the intention behind invoking a “culture war” against feminism, abortion rights, progressive governments, left-wing artists, revolutionary intellectuals, etc., is more of a strategic nature. For those who are actually, as ideologues, behind the “culture war” projects are not Buchanan, Francis, De Benoist, or Faye, but Hayek, Friedman, and the rest of the neoliberal economists. The truth is that neoliberalism in Latin America during the late 20th and early 21st centuries was both a resounding failure and a magnificent victory. This apparent contradiction is resolved depending on which social class we are discussing. During that time, the most powerful social classes, economically speaking, managed to accumulate an enormous amount of power and resources, the likes of which have rarely been seen in Latin American history. But such a level of accumulation in societies subjugated by a global imperialist order (such as those in Latin America) necessarily drives the working classes into conditions of material precariousness that are almost unbearable. Mass migration, uprisings, deaths, the loss of a lifetime’s savings, rising crime, and so on were just some of the devastation left in the wake of the neoliberalism driven by the Washington Consensus during that period. In response to the crisis, several centrist, center-left, and even leftist leaders won elections in the region in quick succession: Chávez in Venezuela, Morales in Bolivia, Fernández in Argentina, Correa in Ecuador, Lula in Brazil, Bachelet in Chile, Mujica in Uruguay, etc. They sought to resolve a capitalist economic crisis within the framework of capitalism itself, resorting to approaches that combined Keynesian measures with legislation designed to protect and expand rights, especially for the most marginalized sectors. These were times when (not without contradictions with other political forces, including those of a more traditional left) the economies of these countries improved, thanks in part to high commodity prices on the global market. And with public policies that, in many cases, focused on providing aid and social programs, the situation of millions of Latin Americans clearly improved. Between 2000 and 2012 alone, 56 million Latin American citizens managed to rise out of poverty. Once the storm of discontent against neoliberalism had passed, the ruling classes decided they’d had enough of progressive governments. But to regain absolute control (since they had always maintained the necessary share of power to influence national decisions), they needed to win back the governments, and to do so, they found themselves at a crossroads. They knew that the central argument against center-left governments could not be based solely on the economic downturn that followed the end of high prices for Latin American natural resources, but that it had to be grounded in something more – something that would come across as novel, radical, and a sort of conservative revolutionary ideology. And that is how they found in the “culture war” a niche for ideological propaganda that has had a historic impact on Latin America. In addition to the aforementioned criticisms, they succeeded (through their intellectuals, politicians, influencers, media outlets, social media, and so on) in creating a perceived link between progressivism and corruption, between progressivism and organized crime, and, finally, between progressivism and an alleged erosion of individual freedom. But the truth is that these kinds of strategies can cause political upheaval like that seen in the region in recent years, during which (thanks to the support of national and international tycoons, as well as support from Washington and other governments such as Israel’s) there has been a string of victories for the radical right, which could complete its winning hand next Sunday in Brazil. But in the long term, neoliberalism cannot (nor does it intend to) overcome the contradiction inherent in an economy of this nature in countries with clear relationships of international domination. Thus, at the height of this new wave of neoliberal right-wing movements, the first cracks in ideological stability are already beginning to appear, precisely in the face of a material reality that offers no respite from political rhetoric. The situation of millions of Latin Americans (especially the poorest) is rapidly being complicated by a radical increase in the rate of inequality. The promises made by the new right-wing movements to defeat organized crime show no signs of being a reality or of bringing about clear regional change. Perhaps this is what Nietzsche, another great reactionary, meant when he acknowledged that culture is merely the veneer of something deeper. And that veneer is beginning to wear away very slowly – a process that is nonetheless noticeable if one pays attention.

articles.title: Tanzania’s smallholder farmers set their course in Morogoro
articles.author: Jonis Ghedi Alasow
articles.content: Some 850 smallholder farmers from across mainland Tanzania and Zanzibar met in Morogoro from September 29 to October 1 for the National Smallholder Farmers’ Conference and the 31st Annual General Meeting (AGM) of MVIWATA, the network of Tanzania’s smallholder farmers’ groups. The theme was “Towards Food Sovereignty: Land Security, Agroecology and Economic Justice for Smallholder Farmers” (“Kuelekea Uhuru wa Chakula: Uhakika wa Ardhi, Kilimo Ikolojia na Haki Uchumi kwa Wakulima Wadogo”). The AGM is MVIWATA’s highest body. Founded by farmers in 1993, the organization interacted directly with 58,916 farmers last year, 57% of whom were women, according to its own count. Two days of conference debate precede the AGM, allowing members to debate policy before coming together to decide the way forward. For this year’s AGM, MVIWATA farmers took up the key issues of land, markets, seed and, for the first time, carbon trade. Dr Bashiru Ally, Tanzania’s Minister of Livestock and Fisheries, opened the meeting, saying he had come to listen rather than lecture. He turned quickly to land: conflicts between peasants and pastoralists, he said, had killed at least fifteen people across five regions in September alone. He asked MVIWATA to help the government end the land conflicts. Guests included the ambassadors of Cuba and Palestine, the Eastern and Southern Africa Small-Scale Farmers’ Forum, the Tanzanian Socialist Forum, and Pan Africanism Today, which delivered a message of solidarity on behalf of more than seventy movements and organizations in Africa. MVIWATA also read its statement of solidarity with Palestine and Cuba. MVIWATA delegates attending the National Smallholder Farmers’ Conference and the 31st Annual General Meeting of MVIWATA. Photo: MVIWATA Land discussions dominated the first day. Delegates said the courts were out of reach for most peasant farmers. MVIWATA’s chairperson, Apollo Chamwela, told those attending the AGM that in Magungu village in Kiteto, more than sixty farmers had lost their land when it was allocated for grazing. Subira from Msomero and Salum from Rudewa, both in Kilosa district, described village land taken by outsiders with the collusion of the local officials who should have prevented it. “How can the government take the side of the minority against the majority?” Subira asked. “Where should we run to cry?” The second day of the AGM focused on markets: not markets in the abstract, but the system through which smallholders are made to sell their crops. Under Tanzania’s warehouse receipt system, farmers deliver produce to licensed warehouses, usually through cooperative unions, and it is sold by digital auction on a government-controlled exchange rather than at the farm gate. Delegates described a system in which farmers have little say over the floor price, and in which middlemen registered as farmers, “ghost farmers” in the words of MVIWATA Executive Director Stephen Ruvuga, sit where prices are set and gain at the real farmers’ expense. Officials on the platform conceded that small producers outside the cooperative unions are “falling between the cracks.” The session on seeds addressed the regional seed law before the East African Legislative Assembly. The carbon session, the most heated of the three days, heard delegates from Dodoma, Katavi and Kagera describe companies counting trees and signing open-ended contracts with individual farmers who were given no opportunity to understand or scrutinize what they were signing. On the final day, the conference resolutions were adopted by acclamation. MVIWATA will compile its members’ land grievances and submit them to the government through Dr Bashiru Ally, as he had offered. It will expand its legal aid and follow up on cases stalled with officials. It will document flaws in the crop-marketing system, present them to the authorities, build a seedbank dedicated to indigenous seeds, convene an inclusive forum on carbon trade, and track, analyze and critically engage carbon projects and their effects on farmers. Dr Bashiru Ally, Tanzania’s Minister of Livestock and Fisheries, opens the MVIWATA meeting. Photo: MVIWATA The AGM then turned to the organization’s future. Its strategic plan for 2027–2031 will put agroecology first, keep land access as a priority and make a farmers’ bank the next major task, starting with TZS 20 million raised from members themselves. Self-reliance ran through the proceedings: members debated doubling their own annual fee, and left energized to prioritize instruments through which farmers can continue to defend themselves. The meeting closed with the election of the board that will lead MVIWATA for the next three years. In its 33rd year, MVIWATA left Morogoro with a sharper agenda: a dossier of land grievances to present to the government, a seed bank and a farmers’ bank to build with members’ own resources, and a public position on carbon trade. The new leadership’s first test will be whether the government acts on the dossier, and whether members fund what they voted for. Delegates who spoke from the floor are identified by first name and village; office-holders are named in full.’ Jonis Ghedi-Alasow is the Coordinator of the Pan Africanism Today Secretariat.

articles.title: Netanyahu declares full lockdown of West Bank after two Israeli soldiers killed in Hebron
articles.author: Aseel Saleh
articles.content: Two Palestinian men carried out a shooting attack , targeting a group of Israeli soldiers near the Farsh al-Hawa military checkpoint in the southern West Bank governorate of Hebron on Friday, October 23. According to media reports, the attackers were assassinated by the Israeli forces after engaging in an exchange of fire for about 20 minutes. They were later identified as Firas al-Ju’ba and Hamoudah al-Ju’ba. The attack also resulted in the killing of two Israeli soldiers and the injury of three others. Netanyahu announces refugee-camp model campaign in Hebron and broader West Bank operation In response to the attack, Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu declared a full lockdown in the West Bank and a large-scale operation that will start from the city of Hebron and the neighboring city of Halhul, and further expand to the entire occupied territory. Wearing a bulletproof vest, Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu threatened from Hebron that the Israeli military will apply the “successful and aggressive model” that the Israeli forces used in the Palestinian refugee camps in the north. The operations in those refugee camps already resulted in the displacement of tens of the thousands of Palestinians, the killing of hundreds, the arrest of over 1,000 , and severe damage and destruction of residential buildings, infrastructure, and properties. “We will evacuate the residents, we will go house to house, remove the weapons there, and all terrorist infrastructure will be dealt with and destroyed,” Netanyahu threatened. The Israeli military already began to demolish buildings and homes in Hebron shortly after the attack was carried out. Referring to the West Bank as Judea and Samaria, Netanyahu continued: “The defense minister and I have seen plans for a very extensive IDF operation in Judea and Samaria, the likes of which have not been carried out since the Six-Day War.” The Six-Day War was a brief, intense conflict fought between Israel and a coalition of Arab states, primarily Egypt, Syria, and Jordan in 1967. As a result of the war, Israel occupied Egypt’s Sinai Peninsula, Syria’s Golan Heights, the West Bank, and the Gaza Strip. It also forced 300,000 Palestinians and 100,000 Syrians to flee into neighboring countries. It is worth noting that Netanyahu and Defense Minister Israel Katz have already threatened a possible war in the West Bank in the last couple of weeks. These threats came hand in hand with an unprecedented escalation of settler violence under the protection of Israeli forces across the occupied territory, alongside intensified military raids. Over 79 Palestinians have been killed in the West Bank in 2026, and more than 1,870 others have been injured since the beginning of 2026. Analysts suggest that the escalation in the West Bank aims to push Palestinians towards a confrontation with the Israeli military, a few days before Israel’s legislative elections, scheduled for October 27.
